The functions $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are known as **intermediate variables.** They are independent variables for the function $f(x,y),$ but are themselves dependent on the variable $t.$

One way to consider how $f(x,y)$ depends on $t$ is to draw a tree diagram.

Starting with $f(x,y),$ we draw a branch for each intermediate variable. Then, we draw a branch for both $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ which are both dependent on the variable $t.$

![](images/cd/cdc47e038ecaba62ae612a0ac0bc07067af232353fc4fc169bf4be57b3abbd1f.png)

We then label each branch with the derivative describing how the function changes due to a change in the variable. 

![](images/ec/ece6012e358b5b6920395df88acd8d7037a7b15bed1add1220365ba72bd24cbd.png)

Then, traversing each branch, we compute the product of the derivatives along each branch and place the result at the end of the branch.

![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

Finally, to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t},$ we sum the results for each branch:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t}
 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

This result is called the **multivariable chain rule**." :tutorial/id #uuid "80ad8a26-7d43-52d6-b0ba-e1d04283e5ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4957 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "03fe551f-81c6-5c42-9baf-d6d12895ab47" :step/math-academy-id 30893 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167573}} {:db/id 17592186167573 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166747 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166585 :question/id #uuid "285e2f4a-e8d0-5f5e-a2d2-fe5ba8476358" :question/math-academy-id "e-8256"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5ed13b87-51ab-547d-a9ed-960eda7db24e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048707}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167326} {:db/id 17592186167331} {:db/id 17592186284666} {:db/id 17592186360551} {:db/id 17592186360552} {:db/id 17592186360553} {:db/id 17592186360554} {:db/id 17592186360555} {:db/id 17592186360556} {:db/id 17592186360557} {:db/id 17592186383607} {:db/id 17592186385838}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable"} :step/id #uuid "a6ab275a-61df-5648-811a-176fda344fe5" :step/math-academy-id 30861 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167697}} {:db/id 17592186167697 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168088 :tutorial/content "There is a special case of the multivariable chain rule when $f=f(x,y)$ and $y=g(x).$ 

Notice that $x$ is an independent variable here. Therefore, the chain rule becomes

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}}_{⏟}}_{1}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}

For example, suppose we have

$$
f = f(x,y), \qquad x=g(s,t), \qquad y=h(s,t).
$$

How do we compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}?$ 

First, let's construct a tree diagram.

![](images/ca/ca524eda2e6be3354fcb72bed52fcaf22257073c3228d74850f8226f9ef0af6f.png)

Now, since we're interested in $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s},$ we highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $s:$

![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

If we keep $t$ fixed and differentiate $f$ with respect to $s,$ then according to the chain rule for two intermediate variables and one independent variable, we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial s}.
$$

Similarly, if we wanted to compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t},$ we would highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$

![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

Keeping $s$ fixed and differentiating $f$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial t}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58d189b1-31fb-5b1b-bc4c-cff6be5e2f7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4958 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "2ffafece-1c0b-50f7-a3b1-e1b2d1bada36" :step/math-academy-id 30894 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167575}} {:db/id 17592186167575 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166749 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166587 :question/id #uuid "1491963b-fbd8-57fa-bdde-f2d6705fbb83" :question/math-academy-id "e-8258"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f26d941b-b4b4-591e-b7e0-ae4bbf81e94b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167311} {:db/id 17592186167325} {:db/id 17592186284668} {:db/id 17592186284669} {:db/id 17592186323886} {:db/id 17592186360483} {:db/id 17592186360484} {:db/id 17592186378038} {:db/id 17592186385363} {:db/id 17592186385824} {:db/id 17592186437272} {:db/id 17592186479133}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "60b2ea1e-4b9a-5557-99ae-a83016e785a6" :step/math-academy-id 30863 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167579}} {:db/id 17592186167579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168063 :tutorial/content "We can generalize the chain rule to a multivariable function containing an arbitrary number of intermediate and independent variables.

Consider the multivariable function 

$$
f = f(x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_m)
$$

with $m$ independent variables and, for each $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\},$ the variable 

$$
x_i = g_i(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n)
$$

is a differentiable function of $n$ independent variables. Then,

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t_j} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial t_j} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial t_j} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_m}{\partial t_j}
$$

for $j \in \{1,2,\ldots, n\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba7d2a4-05a6-5e62-8035-2610239633c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4959 :tutorial/title "The Generalized Multivariable Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "9731a04f-c2d1-5342-b940-0313b71ca1eb" :step/math-academy-id 30895 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167576}} {:db/id 17592186167576 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166750 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166588 :question/id #uuid "e535fe44-a3cb-5c11-831c-118b90582c0d" :question/math-academy-id "e-8259"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71c243ca-5d46-58d2-bd16-28075c04d2db" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167328} {:db/id 17592186167329} {:db/id 17592186284670} {:db/id 17592186323885} {:db/id 17592186360507} {:db/id 17592186360508} {:db/id 17592186360509} {:db/id 17592186360510} {:db/id 17592186360511} {:db/id 17592186383614} {:db/id 17592186385370} {:db/id 17592186420996}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables"} :step/id #uuid "26ddca41-ae16-5395-ae11-41c4d70303c6" :step/math-academy-id 30864} {:db/id 17592186168061 :tutorial/content "The chain rule for single variable functions $f=f(x)$ and $x=x(t)$ states that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.
$$

Let's now suppose that $f = f(x,y),$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$ are single-variable functions. How do we find $\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d t}$ in this case?

The functions $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are known as **intermediate variables.** They are independent variables for the function $f(x,y),$ but are themselves dependent on the variable $t.$

One way to consider how $f(x,y)$ depends on $t$ is to draw a tree diagram.

Starting with $f(x,y),$ we draw a branch for each intermediate variable. Then, we draw a branch for both $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ which are both dependent on the variable $t.$

![](images/cd/cdc47e038ecaba62ae612a0ac0bc07067af232353fc4fc169bf4be57b3abbd1f.png)

We then label each branch with the derivative describing how the function changes due to a change in the variable. 

![](images/ec/ece6012e358b5b6920395df88acd8d7037a7b15bed1add1220365ba72bd24cbd.png)

Then, traversing each branch, we compute the product of the derivatives along each branch and place the result at the end of the branch.

![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

Finally, to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t},$ we sum the results for each branch:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t}
 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}
$$

This result is called the **multivariable chain rule**." :tutorial/id #uuid "80ad8a26-7d43-52d6-b0ba-e1d04283e5ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4957 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186168062 :tutorial/content "How do we apply the multivariable chain rule if the intermediate variables are also dependent on two variables? 

For example, suppose we have

$$

How do we compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s}?$ 

First, let's construct a tree diagram.

Now, since we're interested in $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial s},$ we highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $s:$

![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

If we keep $t$ fixed and differentiate $f$ with respect to $s,$ then according to the chain rule for two intermediate variables and one independent variable, we obtain

Similarly, if we wanted to compute $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t},$ we would highlight all branches that give differentiation with respect to $t\mathbin{:}$

Keeping $s$ fixed and differentiating $f$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "58d189b1-31fb-5b1b-bc4c-cff6be5e2f7b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4958 :tutorial/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule With Two Independent Variables"} {:db/id 17592186168063 :tutorial/content "We can generalize the chain rule to a multivariable function containing an arbitrary number of intermediate and independent variables.

Consider the multivariable function 

$$
f = f(x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_m)
$$

with $m$ independent variables and, for each $i \in \{1,\ldots, n\},$ the variable 

$$

$$

is a differentiable function of $n$ independent variables. Then,

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t_j} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial t_j} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial t_j} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot \dfrac{\partial x_m}{\partial t_j}
$$

for $j \in \{1,2,\ldots, n\}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ba7d2a4-05a6-5e62-8035-2610239633c3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4959 :tutorial/title "The Generalized Multivariable Chain Rule"} {:db/id 17592186168088 :tutorial/content "There is a special case of the multivariable chain rule when $f=f(x,y)$ and $y=g(x).$ 

Notice that $x$ is an independent variable here. Therefore, the chain rule becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot {{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}}_{⏟}}_{1}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "44effd03-02e7-5eb1-8732-ee1522afa147" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5184 :tutorial/title "A Special Case of the Multivariable Chain Rule"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186420998} :activity/id #uuid "844676a2-0a90-5f03-a7c1-22515b371e49" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050031 :topic/id #uuid "27615ef6-ec0e-5e91-b58b-24b70dc01a09" :topic/math-academy-id 3173} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186420997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167325 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a19a158-cb30-5c9e-9cf9-891ab114ad36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(2t-1)" :db/id 17592186355012} {:answer/id #uuid "392f1f1c-1dad-5e72-b1e4-40cf201a767c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}t(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355179} {:answer/id #uuid "869f5f73-0c65-5003-ade6-8eeef3e8b4ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355855} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f0fe58-16c4-5d79-ab11-4893e9ff089a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(s-1)" :db/id 17592186356369} {:answer/id #uuid "fa6ace28-41b6-5a2e-8b64-9dee698d22fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(t-1)" :db/id 17592186356853}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356853} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314b903-87e4-5c8c-a8db-703d520d008b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e1e3cf4a-155f-587d-ba03-cc737759407e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94448" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y,$ where $x=2st$ and $y={s}^{2}t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2cf7698e-82a3-5979-93cb-d2edffbb99d7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421000}} {:db/id 17592186420998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323885 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a9a8991-24fd-50f9-8941-a329e3133c45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+10{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186321230} {:answer/id #uuid "84b790fb-dce2-5ea5-9fbd-fb66967b78c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-20s\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322195} {:answer/id #uuid "bb1f027a-f67b-5d1f-b407-9ee3b85b3667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322598} {:answer/id #uuid "c8bfc905-fde6-54a5-83ad-c5fa1e325d7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322709} {:answer/id #uuid "f675ee7a-8c5d-5a9a-90cb-d0e4dd971fe3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-15s\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186323079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322709} :answer-field/id #uuid "af1de9ae-38d9-5d66-a275-9fc76c319cbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323509}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bd5b5db6-0961-5b1c-8f50-24c2f4348bc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37132" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y-5yz,$ where $x=st,$ $y={s}^{3}$ and $z=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+{c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}st+{c}_{3}s{t}^{4},
$$

find the value of ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "926bef20-92d0-5cd4-928e-9a8dd40763b1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420997}}] :activity/title "The Multivariable Chain Rule" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186420989} {:db/id 17592186420998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323885 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a9a8991-24fd-50f9-8941-a329e3133c45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+10{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186321230} {:answer/id #uuid "84b790fb-dce2-5ea5-9fbd-fb66967b78c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-20s\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322195} {:answer/id #uuid "bb1f027a-f67b-5d1f-b407-9ee3b85b3667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322598} {:answer/id #uuid "c8bfc905-fde6-54a5-83ad-c5fa1e325d7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186322709} {:answer/id #uuid "f675ee7a-8c5d-5a9a-90cb-d0e4dd971fe3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5{s}^{2}{t}^{4}-15s\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t" :db/id 17592186323079}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322709} :answer-field/id #uuid "af1de9ae-38d9-5d66-a275-9fc76c319cbf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323509}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bd5b5db6-0961-5b1c-8f50-24c2f4348bc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-37132" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y-5yz,$ where $x=st,$ $y={s}^{3}$ and $z=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6a9db776-142d-5ace-9b62-834d4e4b6a63" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421001}} {:db/id 17592186420997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167325 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a19a158-cb30-5c9e-9cf9-891ab114ad36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(2t-1)" :db/id 17592186355012} {:answer/id #uuid "392f1f1c-1dad-5e72-b1e4-40cf201a767c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{s}^{2}t(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355179} {:answer/id #uuid "869f5f73-0c65-5003-ade6-8eeef3e8b4ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{s}^{2}(s-t)" :db/id 17592186355855} {:answer/id #uuid "c2f0fe58-16c4-5d79-ab11-4893e9ff089a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(s-1)" :db/id 17592186356369} {:answer/id #uuid "fa6ace28-41b6-5a2e-8b64-9dee698d22fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8st(t-1)" :db/id 17592186356853}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186356853} :answer-field/id #uuid "6314b903-87e4-5c8c-a8db-703d520d008b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e1e3cf4a-155f-587d-ba03-cc737759407e" :question/math-academy-id "q-94448" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y,$ where $x=2st$ and $y={s}^{2}t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}

"f22c7a35-af74-59c8-b71b-cae8347ea97d" :question/math-academy-id "q-37206" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+{z}^{2},$ where $x={s}^{2}+{t}^{2},$ $y=\frac{s}{t}$ and $z=s{t}^{2}.$ Given that

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+{c}_{1}t+{c}_{2}st+{c}_{3}s{t}^{4},
$$

find the value of ${c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{s}{t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(\frac{s}{t})\cdot 2s+({s}^{2}+{t}^{2}+s{t}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(\frac{s}{t}+2s{t}^{2})\cdot {t}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2{s}^{2}}{t}+\frac{{s}^{2}}{t}+t+st+st+2s{t}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3{s}^{2}}{t}+t+2st+2s{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=2,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=1+2+2=5.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "926bef20-92d0-5cd4-928e-9a8dd40763b1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420997}} {:db/id 17592186420999 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284667 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "021a846a-8825-55bf-a7b3-1dc5c5c5ff19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186281709} {:answer/id #uuid "49b2d0a3-8640-5928-a7d2-f8a14102a68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))" :db/id 17592186282314} {:answer/id #uuid "e8a1e1c7-9e8a-5f17-9500-4d7507d44b3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283715} {:answer/id #uuid "efd819c9-60d2-5826-9266-3dba4a49aaec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)}" :db/id 17592186283779} {:answer/id #uuid "f5de75cd-c44e-5baf-9f07-d98f3333edab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186283839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282314} :answer-field/id #uuid "d658fcd0-7d37-5a87-a5b6-42706ffef583" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284307}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cdba7da9-8893-51f6-a38d-eccc847b176c" :question/math-academy-id "q-170670" :question/problem "If $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and $y={x}^{2}+1,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ef0c797-03b2-58eb-8a37-83236f476fe8"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "021a846a-8825-55bf-a7b3-1dc5c5c5ff19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value [{:db/id 17592186231895 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232014 :tutorial/content "So far, we have considered the area of a *right triangle*.
But what is the area of a *general* triangle, one that is not necessarily a right triangle?

It turns out that the same idea still works.

> A formula for the area of a triangle is
> $\textrm{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot b \cdot h$,
> where $b$ is the base and $h$ is the corresponding height.

This formula works for *any* triangle.

Let's use this formula to find the area of the triangle below.

![](images/e7/e7c8eaf780eaa0559e8ac4dc2557a423b805705bfd3a081635f5284502896168.png)

In our triangle,

$$
\textrm{base} = 7 \: \text{ft}, \qquad \textrm{height} = 3 \: \text{ft}
$$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Area &= \frac{1}{2} \cdot 7 \cdot 3 \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \cdot 21 \\
&= 10.5ft^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

At the end of this lesson, we'll show how to prove the formula for the area of a triangle.

Let’s see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "35bf275f-a5b4-5e22-8a11-a01a18b1bd80" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14876 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "A primary school teacher records how many words his second-year students can read in 5 minutes. The number of words read is distributed with a population standard deviation of $\sigma =36$ words. In a school of $180$ students, he finds that the mean number of read words is $255$ words. Find a $95%$ confidence interval for the mean number of words $\mu $ for the entire population of second-year children.

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |" :question/worked-solution "We do not know the distribution of the population. However, the sample size $n=180\ge 30$ is *sufficiently large*. Therefore, according to the central limit theorem, we may use the following approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{―}{X}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- $\mu $ is the population mean,

- ${\sigma }^{2}$ is the population variance, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ of the original distribution is given by

$$
\overset{―}{x}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

In our case,

$$
\overset{―}{x}=255,\,n=180,\,\sigma =36.
$$

We are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.025}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.025})=0.025,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](images/35/35037db1532092651e1974ea689b6004aa673c29720ac1d1c9d191c5929e9314.png)

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.025}=1.96:$ 

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, the $95%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}255\pm 1.96\cdot \frac{36}{\sqrt{180}} \\ 255\pm 5.26\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186499552 :question/id #uuid "e6c6accb-373d-5aa8-b43f-81ebbf038603" :question/math-academy-id "q-142989"} {:db/id 17592186059825 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id Consider a sample of size $n=35$ from a normal population with standard deviation $\sigma =9.4.$ Given that the mean of the sample is $\overset{―}{x}=12.7,$ find a $99%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ of the distribution.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1),$ as shown in the diagram above.*" :question/worked-solution "We are told that the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the distribution of sample mean is also normal, and we have that

$$
\frac{\overset{―}{X}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- $\mu $ is the population mean,

- ${\sigma }^{2}$ is the population variance, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ of the original distribution is given by

$$
\overset{―}{x}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.005}=2.576.
$$

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu $ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 12.7\pm 2.576\cdot \frac{9.4}{\sqrt{35}} \\  & 12.7\pm 4.093\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048944} {:db/id 17592186049866} {:db/id 17592186049985} {:db/id 17592186050936} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f719a65-60e7-57dd-a27a-744f2bd0570e" :answer/type :topic/math-academy-id 260} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060762 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060964 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n=10$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2=9.$ After processing our results, we compute the mean of this sample using the usual methods and get the following result:

$$
\overline{x}=12
$$

 

This is an unbiased estimate of the population mean $\mu.$ However, it is unsatisfactory because we have no information regarding its reliability.

For this reason, it's often more helpful to give a range of possible values for $\mu.$ In other words, instead of reporting a single estimate $\overline{x},$ we might instead report a so-called **confidence interval,** which is an interval of the form

$$
(\overline{x}-E, \: \overline{x}+E)
$$

 

where 

- $\overline{x}$ is our estimate of the population mean, and

- $E$ is some **margin of error**.

In addition, we need to give some indication regarding the reliability of our confidence interval. With this in mind, we will construct a $\boldsymbol{95\%}$ **confidence interval** for the population mean $\mu$. The precise meaning of this will become clear shortly." :tutorial/id #uuid "f8ebcc7b-ddba-56d2-bb41-07916f3c2d09" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6232 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "55b16e12-fb99-528d-a98f-9e754fd27b3a" :step/math-academy-id 37842 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060769}} {:db/id 17592186060763 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059823 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059382 :question/id #uuid "97c8f1dc-747e-5aa4-ab4f-eb809abb560e" :question/math-academy-id "e-10035"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fb626c84-db31-5e1b-90cb-3f5d13ee0af5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049014}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060050} {:db/id 17592186060053} {:db/id 17592186498533} {:db/id 17592186498542} {:db/id 17592186498559} {:db/id 17592186498580} {:db/id 17592186499458} {:db/id 17592186499553}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "bc49103b-afb3-574a-8efd-6910f8c3b320" :step/math-academy-id 37861 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060764}} {:db/id 17592186060764 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059824 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059383 :question/id #uuid "3189a42a-200e-5caa-bc76-6ac1f4ae424d" :question/math-academy-id "e-10039"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "27d20d28-3fba-5830-8bff-76e9a1c24bec" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060051} {:db/id 17592186060054} {:db/id 17592186498524} {:db/id 17592186498543} {:db/id 17592186498557} {:db/id 17592186498576} {:db/id 17592186499443} {:db/id 17592186499552}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals: Applications"} :step/id #uuid "32d40006-ed8e-530b-8e5f-6ec28697e1f4" :step/math-academy-id 37883} {:db/id 17592186060765 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060965 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've assumed that the underlying population is normally distributed. However, if we have a *sufficiently large* sample, then according to the central limit theorem, we can use the approximation

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \approx N(0,1).
$$

So, even though we might not know the underlying distribution, we can still use our formula for the confidence interval of the population mean $\mu{:}$

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4b9c6c26-d589-5847-a384-c431ad44a125" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6245 :tutorial/title "Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "043270f2-b372-59f5-98a2-64919b13fa7b" :step/math-academy-id 37884 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060763}} {:db/id 17592186060766 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060966 :tutorial/content "It's important to be able to interpret confidence intervals correctly.

Imagine we conduct several independent random samples from a population. The mean of the sample will be different for each sample. Some values of $\overline{x}$ might lie close to the population mean $\mu,$ and some could lie further away.

Suppose we construct a $90\%$ confidence interval for each sample and plot them on the same diagram. We might get a picture similar to the one below.

![](images/fc/fc8dd707751cd9e1cb0da1bf618b6d7aed740fab875d8d49c7c89fc09b77321e.png)

In the diagram above, we see that nine out of ten of our confidence intervals contain $\mu,$ while one of them (the red one) does *not* contain the population mean $\mu.$ 

The idea is that if we construct many $90\%$ confidence intervals, one for each sample, then approximately $90\%$ of these confidence intervals will contain the population mean $\mu.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d71a924b-5f1e-5a89-a56b-d540a4a53d74" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6247 :tutorial/title "Interpreting Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "5f0968c6-9ace-5735-9d92-61ff226b832e" :step/math-academy-id 37890 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060765}} {:db/id 17592186060767 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059825 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059384 :question/id #uuid "3a166c80-cc70-5dd3-9dbe-2798dc882199" :question/math-academy-id "e-10046"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b90997d0-b563-5541-9fe2-36d7457da7b5" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049180} {:db/id 17592186049652}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060052} {:db/id 17592186060055} {:db/id 17592186498501} {:db/id 17592186498508} {:db/id 17592186498518} {:db/id 17592186498562} {:db/id 17592186498573} {:db/id 17592186499492} {:db/id 17592186499548}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Normal Populations"} :step/id #uuid "3461449b-03e6-5f5d-aff8-7cec85835701" :step/math-academy-id 37913 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060766}} {:db/id 17592186060768 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060967 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $Z \sim N(0,1).$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score

- $E = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/58/581fc2da88e4419e78389a1b5eedb127f590641d0b7ee21c489ed85184795b13.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "cdae1125-df9d-525c-823d-64f129c3ab6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6275 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Known Population Variance"} :step/id #uuid "afbe0be3-1d3c-5408-9cda-36c61677f0fb" :step/math-academy-id 38032 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060767}} {:db/id 17592186060769 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060968 :tutorial/content "In our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have

$$
Z = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1).
$$

We wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)

  

To help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\alpha.$ Since we're computing a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.
$$

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)

  

According to our diagram,

$$
P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025.
$$

  

Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96.$ Therefore,

$$
P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025.
$$

In other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.96<Z<1.96)=0.95.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96).$

Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1.96< & \,Z<1.96 \\ -1.96< & \,\frac{\overset{―}{x}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}<1.96 \\ -1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\overset{―}{x}-\mu <1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ -\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,-\mu \,<-\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}> & \,\mu >\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\mu <\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=10, \qquad
\overline{x}=12, \qquad
\sigma=3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big).
$$

 

Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "609f60a5-fbfd-5385-89e2-f80dd6281f39" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6398 :tutorial/title "Constructing Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "e659ed87-b26a-54f6-bb76-e98cf99a6b01" :step/math-academy-id 38686 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060768}}] :activity/title "Confidence Intervals for One Mean: Known Population Variance" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186059935} {:db/id 17592186060762 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060964 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n=10$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2=9.$ After processing our results, we compute the mean of this sample using the usual methods and get the following result:

$$
\left(\overline{x} - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \: \overline{x} + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

where $P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},$ and $Z \sim N(0,1).$ 

The endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by

$$
\overline{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Each part of the formula above has a name:

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean

- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score

- $E = z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error

![](images/58/581fc2da88e4419e78389a1b5eedb127f590641d0b7ee21c489ed85184795b13.svg)

So, our confidence interval can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\overset{―}{x}-[\text{margin of error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{margin of error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}], & \,\overset{―}{x}+[\text{[math]z[/math]-score}]\cdot [\text{standard error}]) \\ (\overset{―}{x}-{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}, & \,\overset{―}{x}+{z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}})\end{aligned}
$$

Since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "cdae1125-df9d-525c-823d-64f129c3ab6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6275 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Known Population Variance"} :step/id #uuid "afbe0be3-1d3c-5408-9cda-36c61677f0fb" :step/math-academy-id 38032 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060767}} {:db/id 17592186060967 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\mu$ and *known* population variance $\sigma^2.$ Then, for a given value $\alpha$ between $0$ and $1,$ a $[100(1-\alpha)]\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

Therefore, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where

$$
\overline{X}\sim N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

By transforming $\overline{X}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have

$$
Z = \dfrac{\overline{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\sim N(0,1).
$$

We wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:

![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)

  

To help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\alpha.$ Since we're computing a $95\%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.
$$

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)

  

According to our diagram,

$$
P(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025.
$$

  

Using a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96.$ Therefore,

$$
P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025.
$$

In other words,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.96<Z<1.96)=0.95.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore, there is a $95\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96).$

Now, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\mu\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1.96< & \,Z<1.96 \\ -1.96< & \,\frac{\overset{―}{x}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}}<1.96 \\ -1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\overset{―}{x}-\mu <1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ -\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,-\mu \,<-\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}> & \,\mu >\overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}} \\ \overset{―}{x}-1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}< & \,\mu <\overset{―}{x}+1.96\cdot \frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\mu$ is given by

$$
\left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)
$$

Finally, substituting our values

$$
n=10, \qquad
\overline{x}=12, \qquad
\sigma=3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big).
$$

 

Now that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "609f60a5-fbfd-5385-89e2-f80dd6281f39" :tutorial/math-academy-id D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)},

$$
y=2x\,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2}
$$

The function $x=\sqrt{y}+1$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=1$ and $y=4.$ So, we have $1\le y\le 4.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](images/c5/c55d5f809462b767122ccc4af97c5b4d243730ed24f655bdc18e35ec57e25ce2.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=\frac{y}{2}$ and leaves through the upper function $x=\sqrt{y}+1.$ So, we have $\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}+1.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 4,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}+1}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186339049 :question/id #uuid "efbcfea6-0f26-55f3-9790-4f12e94364d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-72049" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "099efdac-6222-5744-b3c1-1dad27d41b85" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the listed" :db/id 17592186336117} {:answer/id #uuid "2f51b9b3-9edb-5ad5-a10c-52cfdfd9e751" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/6c/6ccd325f24c9550f82a7063623db1cae0212a07f1c938b882c6707d35a6eee29.png" :db/id 17592186336484} {:answer/id #uuid "5a4f7dba-2306-55b0-ad53-f7348ae38b3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/5a/5a14be084ba22e33b636465156276fc489904a650077612c15fdec3634f8d902.png" :db/id 17592186336855} {:answer/id #uuid "d8f500b5-47d1-5c54-82d7-03d7175ff4bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/5e/5e41509dcb689a5f16822eea9b8700171a74124789e12990ee4fd292d52aa2ea.png" :db/id 17592186337919} {:answer/id #uuid "f39c32b9-aa95-5261-a245-c6851bf03b8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/81/81b206d34bfa12b8623329616368ea3e6a978cf7963dbe5f09b23cafffb76dae.png" :db/id 17592186338160}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186336484} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0492a08-2d29-5eca-af88-ac3ff00ea955" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186338600}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following is a type II region in two-dimensional space?" :question/worked-solution "A type II region can be written as

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?" :question/worked-solution "A type II region can be written as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)\},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $y:$

$$
y={e}^{x-1}\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1
$$

The function $x=0$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=1$ and $y=e.$ So, we have $1\le y\le e.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](images/68/680842905f6e308d3c438063769bde9854401a300371452d1c0735bb7d272a02.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=0$ and leaves through the upper function $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1.$ So, we have $0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le e,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1\}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435897 :question/id #uuid "ed99a179-e753-5cd2-8fc5-79553f622379" :question/math-academy-id "q-168840"} {:db/id 17592186129169 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $$

$$

$$

$$

:topic/math-academy-id 1979} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186130023 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130371 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the region that lies between the curves ${\color{red}y=f(x)}$ and ${\color{blue}y=g(x)}$ over a closed interval $[a,b]$ on the $x$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/a4/a45abf7904382a16daaa38ff617a9487b5c274cf65ef44f89e7feb0c32c496e0.png)

This region is an example of a **type I region**. Generally, a type I region is any region bounded by two vertical lines $x=a$ and $x=b,$ and two curves $y=g(x)$ and $y=f(x),$ where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions. 

Using set notation, a type I region can be written as

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq x  \leq b, \quad g(x) \leq y \leq f(x) \big\}.
$$

In a type I region, any vertical line drawn through the region should intersect the region in a *single* interval, as shown below.

![](images/f7/f7282efbe2c9244c77ce6bbbeca047ee3ab29dd2fc90e0d2440c519328cb5973.png)

By contrast, the following region is *not* a type I region since there is a vertical line whose intersection with the region results in two *separate* line segments. In other words, the vertical line enters and leaves the region more than once.

![](images/a2/a26c7588e297a8af35f1e709210596a94f3fb4bd84e8237dc1462f48b961630e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "2658cc5e-d169-5ff8-871c-4ccaab428eb7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3854 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0b518252-fe1c-57d7-bc6f-6a00d3addac9" :step/math-academy-id 22589 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130024}} {:db/id 17592186130024 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129167 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128986 :question/id #uuid "9cbb7321-753d-5253-8b64-072e3cc227bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-6101"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "64d342be-ebaf-5e94-b641-ea8ce6f14c12" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049051} {:db/id 17592186050367} {:db/id 17592186050641}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129837} {:db/id 17592186129838} {:db/id 17592186339048} {:db/id 17592186342004} {:db/id 17592186374248} {:db/id 17592186375307} {:db/id 17592186375314} {:db/id 17592186375328} {:db/id 17592186393187} {:db/id 17592186429974} {:db/id 17592186435896}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Type I Regions"} :step/id #uuid "1b6899de-a336-56a9-809a-31cc01aeebb8" :step/math-academy-id 22590 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130025}} {:db/id 17592186130025 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130372 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the region that lies between the curves ${\color{red}x=f(y)}$ and ${\color{blue}x=g(y)}$ over a closed interval $[a,b]$ on the $y$-axis, as shown below.

![](images/cf/cf2a2a41d63f21b279215fd1aa8d7361eb638e831b970bb3de861673f67612e6.png)

This region is an example of a **type II region**. In general, a type II region is any region that is bounded by two horizontal lines $y=a$ and $y=b,$ and two curves $x=g(y)$ and $x=f(y),$ where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

Using set notation, a type II region can be written as

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq y  \leq b, \quad g(y) \leq x \leq f(y) \big\}.
$$

In a type II region, any horizontal line drawn through the region should intersect the region in a *single* interval, as shown below.

![](images/a4/a45abf7904382a16daaa38ff617a9487b5c274cf65ef44f89e7feb0c32c496e0.png)

This region is an example of a **type I region**. Generally, a type I region is any region bounded by two vertical lines $x=a$ and $x=b,$ and two curves $y=g(x)$ and $y=f(x),$ where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions. 

Using set notation, a type I region can be written as

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq x  \leq b, \quad g(x) \leq y \leq f(x) \big\}.
$$

In a type I region, any vertical line drawn through the region should intersect the region in a *single* interval, as shown below.

![](images/f7/f7282efbe2c9244c77ce6bbbeca047ee3ab29dd2fc90e0d2440c519328cb5973.png)

By contrast, the following region is *not* a type I region since there is a vertical line whose intersection with the region results in two *separate* line segments. In other words, the vertical line enters and leaves the region more than once.

Select all that apply.

- **I.** It is a type I region
- **II.** It is a type II region
- **III.** It's neither a type I nor a type II region" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}y={x}^{3}\, & ⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y} \\ y=\sqrt[3]{x}\, & ⟹\,x={y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/89/899357795c6d5b81d3cb619d71493ad787645697fe1f2fcecda78c1b875f388e.png)

We have the following:

- Any vertical line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{3}\le y\le \sqrt[3]{x}}.
$$

So, this is a type I region.

- Any horizontal line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,{y}^{3}\le x\le \sqrt[3]{y}}.
$$

So, this is a type II region.

Therefore, only statements I and II are true."} :step/id #uuid "fd242e61-69b5-5bfd-bc83-d7379d3f45c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406986}} {:db/id 17592186406986 :step/content {:db/id 17592186339070 :question/math-academy-id "q-72344" :question/problem "![](images/40/4066b07ace047e9a7ce813ed70dd6648649a192d648ed810fa96b5146d2c5581.png)

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?" :question/worked-solution "A type II region can be written as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)\},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $y:$

$$
y={e}^{x-1}\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1
$$

The function $x=0$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=1$ and $y=e.$ So, we have $1\le y\le e.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](images/68/680842905f6e308d3c438063769bde9854401a300371452d1c0735bb7d272a02.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=0$ and leaves through the upper function $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1.$ So, we have $0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le e,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1\}.

$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/09/0960063edcce8ccd55dc2f77147c4a4982645c180e8b998d7e520c65131ea045.png)

$$

- Any horizontal line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\le x\le \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\}.
$$

So, this is a type II region.

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?" :question/worked-solution "A type II region can be written as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)\},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $y:$

$$
y={e}^{x-1}\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1
$$

The function $x=0$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=1$ and $y=e.$ So, we have $1\le y\le e.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](images/68/680842905f6e308d3c438063769bde9854401a300371452d1c0735bb7d272a02.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=0$ and leaves through the upper function $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1.$ So, we have $0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le e,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{ln}⁡(y)+1\}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3390ee50-86eb-5461-9633-3fe230269903" :step/next {:db/id 17592186429978}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "177be529-dbfe-5550-a65b-a03b4c722a7b" :answer/type {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1\, & ⟹\,x=\pm \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1\, & ⟹\,y=\pm \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/09/0960063edcce8ccd55dc2f77147c4a4982645c180e8b998d7e520c65131ea045.png)

We have the following:

- Any vertical line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\le y\le \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\}.
$$

So, this is a type I region.

- Any horizontal line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\le x\le \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\}.
$$

So, this is a type II region.

Roots of a Rational Function With a Linear Numerator and No Common Factors"}] :question/problem "Solve $f(x)=0$, where $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x^2 + x - 6}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we factor $f(x)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= \frac{2x + 1}{x^{2} + x - 6} \\
&= (2x + 1)/((x + 3)(x - 2))
\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x + 1 &= 0 \\
2x &= -1 \\
x &= -\frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to

$$
f(x)=0
$$

is

$$
x=-\dfrac{1}{2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048673} {:db/id 17592186049074} {:db/id 17592186055163 :question/id #uuid "c08dc52d-2b09-547b-9d67-555b643c2206" :question/math-academy-id "q-24667"} {:db/id 17592186055471 :question/id #uuid "d485eff6-e95b-5c68-aab9-92c4dd571413" :question/math-academy-id "q-70496"} {:db/id 17592186054740 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054555 :question/id #uuid "bf127b16-01c5-58c9-903a-e00fe349c011" :question/math-academy-id "e-5139"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d98f7bd-2351-5eb8-80ff-67adcba4adbc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049244}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055167 :question/id #uuid "2e94a787-0884-5fb4-b10a-d7ca4c6ce094" :question/math-academy-id "q-24674"} {:db/id 17592186055170 :question/id #uuid "48614460-9755-5fd1-aa64-ddc77080ea8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-24969"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With a Quadratic Numerator and No Common Factors"} {:db/id 17592186054555 :question/id #uuid "bf127b16-01c5-58c9-903a-e00fe349c011" :question/math-academy-id "e-5139" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054740 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d98f7bd-2351-5eb8-80ff-67adcba4adbc" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With a Quadratic Numerator and No Common Factors"}] :question/problem "Solve $f(x)=0$, where $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2-4x}{x^2+5x+6}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we factor $f(x)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}

&= (x(x - 4))/((x + 2)(x + 3))
\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(x - 4) &= 0 \\
x &= 0, 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to

$$
f(x)=0
$$

are $x=0$ and $x=4$."} {:db/id 17592186049244} {:db/id 17592186055167 :question/id #uuid "2e94a787-0884-5fb4-b10a-d7ca4c6ce094" :question/math-academy-id "q-24674"} {:db/id 17592186055170 :question/id #uuid "48614460-9755-5fd1-aa64-ddc77080ea8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-24969"} {:db/id 17592186054741 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054554 :question/id #uuid "f4a45939-a80c-5e3e-bf2f-b3097a42c2ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-5137"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e77fe2f6-0e93-5378-aa8d-cc6d5122bdaa" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050323}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055161 :question/id #uuid "bc462294-a423-56b8-98fb-24f656b8a59a" :question/math-academy-id "q-24655"} {:db/id 17592186055164 :question/id #uuid "dede4879-61c2-5a6e-a952-d9622fd9143f" :question/math-academy-id "q-24671"} {:db/id 17592186055165 :question/id #uuid "d0ab5d8c-b596-5c6f-9662-1d4d7f714f74" :question/math-academy-id "q-24672"} {:db/id 17592186233162 :question/id #uuid "00a59e1b-5af6-5ac9-a60d-0391a4287a61" :question/math-academy-id "q-113092"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With Common Factors"} {:db/id 17592186054554 :question/id #uuid "f4a45939-a80c-5e3e-bf2f-b3097a42c2ff" :question/math-academy-id "e-5137" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054741 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e77fe2f6-0e93-5378-aa8d-cc6d5122bdaa" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With Common Factors"}] :question/problem "Solve $f(x)=0$, where $f(x) = \dfrac{x+1}{x^2-x-2}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= \frac{x^{3} - 2x^{2} - 9x + 18}{x^{2} - x - 2} \\
&= (x^{2}(x - 2) - 9(x - 2))/((x - 2)(x + 1)) \\
&= ((x - 2)(x^{2} - 9))/((x - 2)(x + 1)) \\
&= ((x - 2)(x - 3)(x + 3))/((x - 2)(x + 1)) \\
&= ((x - 2)(x - 3)(x + 3))/((x - 2)(x + 1)) \\
&= ((x - 3)(x + 3))/(x + 1)

:step/math-academy-id 34281 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189120}} {:db/id 17592186189095 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189371 :tutorial/content "To compute the expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ given a joint mass function $f(x,y),$ we must first find its marginal mass function $f_X.$ Once the marginal mass function is known, we can then compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ using the formula

$$
\textrm{E}[X]
= \sum\limits_{i=1}^n x_i \, f_X(x_i).
$$

For example, consider the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y,$ shown below.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ |

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Since we're only interested in the expected value of $X,$ let's compute the row totals only.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.05$ | $0.15$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.20}$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0.80}$ |

Therefore, the marginal mass function of $X$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f_X(x)$ | $0.20$ | $0.80$ |
|  |  |  |

We can now compute the expected value of $X\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\  & =1\cdot 0.2+2\cdot 0.8 \\  & =0.2+1.6 \\  & =1.8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\textrm{E}[X] = 1.8.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0512a52f-ccb2-56a2-b436-f49ec9cb4916" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6253 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3c190be0-696c-59a8-9758-3931bd0f72ac" :step/math-academy-id 37912 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189081}} {:db/id 17592186189115 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188296 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188003 :question/id #uuid "f32f96bc-b02a-54fe-b370-8a384c6ae67e" :question/math-academy-id "e-10102"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7447ccfe-83a7-59d4-8386-c74a3ab47b89" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049553} {:db/id 17592186049801}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188538} {:db/id 17592186188564} {:db/id 17592186478374} {:db/id 17592186478405} {:db/id 17592186478427} {:db/id 17592186478451} {:db/id 17592186478463}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Expected Value of a Continuous Random Variable From a Joint Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "595885fa-5146-5a3a-8643-30f924026039" :step/math-academy-id 38102} {:db/id 17592186189120 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189382 :tutorial/content "To compute the expected value of a *continuous* random variable $X$ given a joint density function $f(x,y),$ we must first find its marginal density function $f_X.$ Once the marginal density function is known, we can then compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ using the formula

:step/content {:db/id 17592186065394 :tutorial/content "Derivatives naturally occur in many real-world situations, so it's essential to know their units of measurement. The key is to remember that the derivative represents a rate of change.

For instance, suppose that the temperature of a pizza $t$ minutes after coming out of a hot oven is $T(t)$ degrees Fahrenheit. What are the units of $\dfrac{\textrm{d}T}{\textrm{d}t}?$

First, we have that the temperature $T(t)$ is measured in degrees Fahrenheit and the time $t$ is measured in minutes.

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t): & \text{degrees Fahrenheit} \\ t: & \text{minutes}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\color{black}T}{\textrm{d}\color{black}t}$ measures a change in ${\color{black}T}$ over a change in ${\color{black}t}.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}: & \frac{\text{degrees Fahrenheit}}{\text{minutes}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\color{black}T}{\textrm{d}\color{black}t}$ is measured in "degrees Fahrenheit per minute", or $^\circ \textrm F / \textrm {min}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Adding or subtracting a value to the graph of $y=\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^x$ will **translate** (shift) the graph up or down the $y$-axis. 

For instance, $y=\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^x+3$ has the same shape as $y=\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^x,$ but it's shifted $3$ units up.

![](images/f7/f76f7a276392996811bd70c707107c3b8e3e764c38d188ae3e31e4414ad92ff2.png)

Note the following points:

- The $y$-intercept $(0,1)$ has moved up $3$ units to the point $(0,4).$

- The horizontal asymptote $y=0$ has moved up $3$ units to $y=3.$

Now, consider the graph of $y=\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^x-3.$ In this case, the graph of $y=\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^x$ is shifted $3$ units *down*.

![](images/7e/7e5afd3739b8db7488041a8c90fc0ca7db1e61908ffd7bf7ca4d484fa356f5eb.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "2643e949-fb98-521b-81d0-fd82217dfc2e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1546 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "32de2f5b-55c5-5708-a384-5a4d3bc02ea7" :step/math-academy-id 3945 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069766}} {:db/id 17592186069766 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068829 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068454 :question/id #uuid "da62e401-d03d-54fd-90b5-410d36bdefad" :question/math-academy-id "e-1226"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5bb394c3-cd7c-523d-88df-b1306d9d528f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048295} {:db/id 17592186049660}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069196} {:db/id 17592186069198} {:db/id 17592186297326} {:db/id 17592186297335} {:db/id 17592186390531} {:db/id 17592186390592}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Vertically Shifted Exponential Decay Curve"} :step/id #uuid "fe3a1979-05f3-5832-b489-34e3e8ebfc22" :step/math-academy-id 3946 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069874}} {:db/id 17592186069767 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069939 :tutorial/content "When an exponential decay function is vertically shifted *and* stretched, we apply the stretch first and the shift second.

For example, to plot the function $y=2\left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right)^x+3,$ we start by plotting the graph of $y = \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right)^x{:}$

![](images/84/842f4b6dfd9a45f4d187f4b448048879761cfbf4d880a113c9f3fcabc4988543.png)

Next, we plot the graph of $y = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^x.$ To do this, we scale the graph above by a factor of $2.$ The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to $(0,2)$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](images/04/0439fee0ab5e8e993cd5eda5dbebc72e5b79209c60aa547c036940ced6a970eb.png)

Finally, we plot the graph of $y = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^x + 3.$ To do this, we shift the above graph $3$ units above. The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,2)$ to $(0,5)$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from $y=0$ to $y=3.$

\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\sech x)' = -\sech x\tanh x, \quad (\csch x)' = -\csch x \coth x, \quad (\coth x)' = -\csch^2 x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results and the rules of differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(3sech x + \coth x) \\
&= 3\frac{d}{dx}(sech x) + \frac{d}{dx}(\coth x) \\
&= 3(-sech x\tanh x) + (-csch^{2} x) \\
&=-3sech x\tanh x - csch^{2} x
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048192} {:db/id 17592186167341 :question/id #uuid "ea9f8f07-a38b-5320-8a01-10ad61981f4b" :question/math-academy-id "q-95282" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166761 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "597e3939-e6b4-5237-a16e-8bae92f9b656" :knowledge-point/title "Basic Derivatives of the Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8391f1f9-d35b-5902-a485-f98123940971" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\coth x(csch x - Find the derivative of $f(x) =\coth(5x - 2)$." :question/worked-solution "$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f =\coth{g}, \qquad g = 5x - 2
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} = -\csch^2{g}
$$

and

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x} = 5
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{df}{dx} &= -csch^{2} g \cdot 5 \\
&=-5csch^{2} g \\
&=-5csch^{2} (5x - 2)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186051084} {:db/id 17592186167342 :question/id #uuid "4961c69f-36e3-58cb-9210-1bf156b37d00" :question/math-academy-id "q-95284"} {:db/id 17592186167390 :question/id #uuid "53325a1f-060f-5563-8089-8adc0f47a0e5" :question/math-academy-id "q-95574"} {:db/id 17592186166763 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166601 :question/id #uuid "4baa8799-f8ce-521e-833b-8b66c747e701" :question/math-academy-id "e-8351"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a991a2f4-b96a-5f92-8b52-6102647be98e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048813}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167343 :question/id #uuid "5cd7acb2-13d4-5813-bdef-217cf5d07814" :question/math-academy-id "q-95285"} {:db/id 17592186167393 :question/id #uuid "64faafa8-6050-5000-989e-ec74aea34356" :question/math-academy-id "q-95584"}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Product Rule"} {:db/id 17592186166601 :question/id #uuid "4baa8799-f8ce-521e-833b-8b66c747e701" :question/math-academy-id "e-8351" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186166763 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a991a2f4-b96a-5f92-8b52-6102647be98e" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Product Rule"}] :question/problem "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}$

Find the derivative of $f(x) = x^2\coth{x}$." :question/worked-solution "$$
\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits} \newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits} \newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}
$$

Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x) = x^2$ and

$$
v(x) = \coth{x}
$$

So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{′}(x) &= (x^{2})^{′} \cdot \coth x + x^{2} \cdot (\coth x)^{′} \\
&= 2x \cdot \coth x + x^{2} \cdot (-csch^{2} x) \\
&= x(2\coth x - xcsch^{2} x)
