$$
15\div 4 = 3\,\textrm{R} \color{blue}{3}
$$

$$
\textrm{i}^{15} = \textrm{i}^{\color{blue}{3}} = -\textrm{i}

\textrm{i}^{7}$, then $ab =$" :question/worked-solution "Using the addition law for exponents, we have

$$
ab =\textrm{i}^9\cdot\textrm{i}^7 = \textrm{i}^{9+7} = \textrm{i}^{16}
$$

To find the value of $\textrm{i}$ raised to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=16$. Dividing the power by $4$, we get

$$
16\div 4 = 4\,\textrm{R} \color{blue}{0}
$$

So the remainder is $\color{blue}0$. Therefore,

$$
\textrm{i}^{16} = \textrm{i}^{\color{blue}{0}} =1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050668} {:db/id 17592186050697} {:db/id 17592186055399 :question/id #uuid "95d475b7-c1b7-528f-9642-f10b5011ab3d" :question/math-academy-id "q-571"} {:db/id 17592186055515 :question/problem "Find the value of $\textrm{i}^{-2}$." :question/worked-solution "First, using the laws of exponents, we can write

$$
\textrm{i}^{-2}=\dfrac{1}{\textrm{i}^2}
$$

We now recall that

$$
\textrm{i}^2 = -1
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{1}{\textrm{i}^2} = \dfrac{1}{(-1)} = -1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050495} {:db/id 17592186055460 :question/id #uuid "3fd6c093-c85b-59ae-9645-c6c1fdf717b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-66488"} {:db/id 17592186055461 :question/id #uuid "a5bf802d-deab-55c9-9615-fe3a251904e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-66489"} {:db/id 17592186233161 :question/id #uuid "78b80ccb-1ed2-5f38-b3d6-5f94447df807" :question/math-academy-id "q-113087"} {:db/id 17592186234202 :question/id #uuid "af7b42e4-11d8-5986-a8ac-7aad3c2b5d40" :question/math-academy-id "q-66490"} {:db/id 17592186234213 :question/id #uuid "c85e6509-8a4c-5c95-930a-ad19c0b94bec" :question/math-academy-id "q-66874"} {:db/id 17592186049702} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186055535} :activity/id #uuid "a56c5450-2be5-51a0-b60f-0dfe05b153cc" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050218 :topic/id #uuid "370d229e-4b9a-5ee8-b857-c25ac383bf2c" :topic/math-academy-id 32} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055532 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055965 :tutorial/content "Let's remind ourselves of the first few powers of $\textrm{i}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\textrm{i}^{1} &= \textrm{i} \\
\textrm{i}^{2} &= -1 \\
\textrm{i}^{3} &= -\textrm{i} \\
\textrm{i}^{4} &= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

At the fourth power, we return to the value of $1$, which can also be written as

$$
\textrm{i}^0 = 1
$$

This means that if we continue to increase the powers, we would cycle through the same four values once again, as shown below.

![](images/5e/5e3f3a42dd591daf109e474eec99e446706e0d8e46f1252540839cd50d957463.png)

So, for $\textrm{i}^5$ through $\textrm{i}^8$, the exact same pattern repeats. Remembering that

$$
\textrm{i}^4 = 1
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned} \textrm{i}^5&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i} \\[5pt] \textrm{i}^6&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1 \\[5pt] \textrm{i}^7&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \\[5pt] \textrm{i}^8&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1. \end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, for $\textrm{i}^9$ through to $\textrm{i}^{12}$, the pattern repeats again:

$$
\begin{aligned} \textrm{i}^9&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i} \\[5pt] \textrm{i}^{10}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1 \\[5pt] \textrm{i}^{11}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \\[5pt] \textrm{i}^{12}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to simplify a higher integer power of $\textrm{i}$, we *divide the power by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder*.

17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+3 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3-2s}{s(s-1)},\,$
${X}_{2}(s)=$ {{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{{x}_{1}(t)+3\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{3}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-1=-{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\},$ and we have used the fact that $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the first equation for ${X}_{1}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2 & ={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{3}{s} \\ (s-1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3}{s}-2 \\ (s-1){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3-2s}{s} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3-2s}{s(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)-1 & =-{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =1-{X}_{1}(s) \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =1-(\frac{3-2s}{s(s-1)}) \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s(s-1)-3+2s}{s(s-1)} \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-s-3+2s}{s(s-1)} \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+s-3}{s(s-1)} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+s-3}{s(s-1)(s-3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system  in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3-2s}{s(s-1)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}+s-3}{s(s-1)(s-3)}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167232 :question/id #uuid "968c34ea-6536-56be-a722-82e75e44e26e" :question/math-academy-id "q-333064"} {:db/id 17592186305119 :question/id #uuid "53d3abf7-a9e9-5b69-8cf5-e63a711cb51d" :question/math-academy-id "q-332784"} {:db/id 17592186308369 :question/id #uuid "e3c4c091-3098-5cdd-a98e-d6a345ec5978" :question/math-academy-id "q-333070" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0039aee6-98b7-59c0-8d03-5b2d50aa3e57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3(s+2)}{s(s-2)(s-5)}" :db/id 17592186305152}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305152} :answer-field/id #uuid "0377913c-e842-526c-a0d1-86f1c0379261" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307528}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=$ {{field-1}},$\,$
${X}_{2}(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{5{x}_{2}(t)+2\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=5L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}+2L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-0=2{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-1=5{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\},$ and we have used the fact that $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the second equation for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)-1 & =5{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{2}{s} \\ (s-5){X}_{2}(s) & =1+\frac{2}{s} \\ (s-5){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s+2}{s} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the first equation and solving for ${X}_{1}(s)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s) & =2{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =3(\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}) \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3(s+2)}{s(s-5)(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3(s+2)}{s(s-2)(s-5)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.

\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+3 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}=\frac{1}{s-1}-\frac{3}{s},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}=\frac{1/2}{s-1}-\frac{1}{s}+\frac{3/2}{s-3}.
$$

$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t}-3 \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{t}+\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}-1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

"![](images/0b/0bebe0003d3d70b77be931f2dba651d85352bddf6e41b94055bb227b07d60153.svg)

**Step 1**. In the initial value problem above, we apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation.

First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{{x}_{1}(t)+5\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)-2\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+5L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+4L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-2L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the result

$$
\mathcal L\{1\} = \dfrac{1}{s},
$$

we can write our system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)-\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}$ are the Laplace transforms of the functions $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t),$ respectively.

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+2={X}_{1}(s)+\frac{5}{s}\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) - 3 = - 2 \left(\dfrac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\right) + 4 X_2(s) - \dfrac{2}{s}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_2(s) = \dfrac{3s^2-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}.
$$

**Step 3**. To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{-2s+5}{s(s-1)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3}{s-1}-\frac{5}{s}\} \\  & =3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\}-5{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =3{e}^{t}-5 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3{s}^{2}-s-8}{s(s-1)(s-4)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2}{s-1}+\frac{3}{s-4}-\frac{2}{s}\} \\  & =2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-1}\}+3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-4}\}-2{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}-5 \\ 2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{4t}-2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "00904ad0-6191-560b-a452-c838aa7543a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14420 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "822d22ea-2253-5461-b518-1ae1ae238fee" Similar to the homogeneous case, the process can be split into three steps.

- **Step 1.** Apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation, to get a system with variables 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.
$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find initial variables 

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)
$$

satisfying the original initial value problem, apply the inverse Laplace transform to 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "3733acd7-1a13-5183-a501-0baf1eaf53a5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14611 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046644} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186506621} :activity/id #uuid "acf80487-30da-5578-b5d8-3413af242da3" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049381 :topic/id #uuid "f0242aed-46fd-5f2e-bcc2-49ee070cdccf" :topic/math-academy-id 3190} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186506606 :step/content {:db/id 17592186506573 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4faa0bc1-0f83-5df5-b327-6631924a3461" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{3t}-3" :db/id 17592186506046}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506046} :answer-field/id #uuid "29a780d4-7f5e-5121-9749-f435d4e070d4" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506399} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "82f32ceb-ba57-523c-9952-b5724c0a4bf7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3e^{2t}-2e^{3t}+1" :db/id 17592186506138}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186506138} :answer-field/id #uuid "31d556ca-1ce9-5f66-b4a1-85148a156058" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186506404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a2d20627-2f13-5baa-ae6b-0096d23c5fcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-333135" :question/problem "$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution 

$$

$$

:step/content {:db/id 17592186055976 :tutorial/content "The **magnitude** of a complex number is its distance from the origin. It's denoted as $\mid z \mid$.

For example, consider the complex number

$$
z=-4+5\textrm{i}
$$

shown in the complex plane below.

![](images/33/33d0294178c15b883f8f4988e34d7c81244edd9f426e9ed206e10469dbc5abf1.png)

Using the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid z \mid &= \sqrt{(-4)^{2} + (5)^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{16 + 25} \\
&= \sqrt{41}
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, for a complex number

$$
z=a+b\textrm{i}
$$

the magnitude of $z$ can be found as follows:

$$
\mid z \mid = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "df0d2109-2954-5b2d-8b02-98a43f80ac89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3329 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "332a5684-42f1-5051-9109-e6eecf07792c" :step/math-academy-id :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186268883 :question/id #uuid "484f8b36-97b4-5e4f-a875-d05f61c48bf6" :question/math-academy-id "q-132585" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "106c62f5-6a15-5356-9819-bac29ddd8e00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=-4x+9\end{aligned}" :db/id 17592186266282} {:answer/id #uuid "4cdcc8ed-799e-5868-8d9c-e5cddb211a2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=-4x+21\end{aligned}" :db/id 17592186266824} {:answer/id #uuid "502e00e2-2746-5fc9-8240-98511ddcf672" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=2x+9\end{aligned}" :db/id 17592186266856} {:answer/id #uuid "50dcaed5-8a14-56a6-9c8d-e4ff85b79e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=-2x+15\end{aligned}" :db/id 17592186266866} {:answer/id #uuid "9b80ced7-aa68-5bf4-8dc4-6402f10538d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=2x+21\end{aligned}" :db/id 17592186267546}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186266824} :answer-field/id #uuid "49d228b2-8aea-57a5-b2ca-483e7c7b3e29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268529}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Given that the point $P(4,-2,5)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=y\sqrt{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(4,-2,5)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(4,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)} & =(-2)\sqrt{4} \\  & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(4,-2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}(x-4) \\ z-5 & =-4(x-4) \\ z & =-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,-2,5)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124439 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124243 :question/id #uuid "75c0deaf-38a7-5a81-afac-cae2978d52b4" :question/math-academy-id "e-3070"} :knowledge-point/id $$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,-3,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

:topic/math-academy-id 1955} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125265 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125723 :tutorial/content "Just as the derivative of a function represents the slope of the tangent line to the function, the partial derivative of a function has a geometric interpretation as well.

To illustrate, consider the surface $z = f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$ and the plane $x=3.$ The intersection of the surface and the plane forms a downward parabolic curve, as shown below. A point $P(3,2,5)$ is plotted and a tangent line is drawn through that point.

![](images/86/8619c41cd0caf04ae9ee9bcae61e31739d8da583793a67c1c87e00186c3ac417.png)

   

To find the slope of the tangent, we can compute the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(18-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =-2y \\ {\frac{∂f}{∂y}|}_{P} & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To verify that this result is correct, we can find the equation of the downward parabolic curve and then use single-variable calculus to compute the slope of the tangent line.

To find the equation of the downward parabolic curve, we can substitute the equation of the plane ($x=3$) into the equation of the surface ($f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$). Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,y) & =18-{3}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\  & =9-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the downward parabolic curve is $z=g(y) = 9-y^2.$ In the $yz$-plane, this curve has the following graph:

![](images/e9/e982ef5d6d8d4fec9c64957d46f22cea2a85bd002595642f58700cf48cce4256.png)

To find the slope of the tangent to $g(y)$ at $P,$ we can use single-variable calculus. We differentiate $g(y)$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(y) & =-2y \\ {g}^{′}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "56aef924-0db1-5d63-a9a3-5a81bcbdc411" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2376 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ef70361b-fe3c-57f6-a037-19f320382e64" :step/math-academy-id $$

$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

$$

$$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)} & =(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+4(0)+(-2) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,0)}(y-0) \\ z-8 & =-4(y-0) \\ z & =-4y+8\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-4y+8\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it."} :step/id #uuid "a1abbae1-4f02-53d9-a1d3-0117fc214a32" :step/next {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,-1) & =(1)^{2}(2(1)(-1)-1)=-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,-1) & ={f}_{y}(1,-1)(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3(y+1) \\ z-2 & =-3y-3 \\ z & =-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,-1,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-3y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-3y-1$ (or $-3y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,-3,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$

:question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=e.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(e,2,3)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(e,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(e,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(e,2) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\frac{{e}^{2}}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(e,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(e,2)}(y-2) \\ z-3 & =1(y-2) \\ z & =y+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(e,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=e \\ z=y+1\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0dfd5f35-4d13-5e8b-b12c-5286da4ef943"} {:db/id 17592186425122 :step/content {:db/id 17592186425118 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09b9a14b-262a-515e-bd82-1f704a821349" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186425090} {:answer/id #uuid "2590094e-7f95-52df-bdd8-abb0af831110" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186425096} {:answer/id #uuid "336e9f14-d6c6-5f83-897b-4c14eb89e5be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186425097} {:answer/id #uuid "91000328-2b30-5049-9390-2fee6404bd0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186425109} {:answer/id #uuid "e4a190e1-968a-5e68-8061-84d550c81b2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186425113}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186425090} :answer-field/id #uuid "4d50699f-3ed7-5626-8b63-c6ce285403be" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186425116}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5cb4c36d-f79b-5525-8cf7-91f3e27f40c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-64966" :question/problem "A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={2}^{x+y}y(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1)$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(0,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(0,1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5 \\ z=x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it."} :step/id #uuid "a385dd67-f4d9-5c4e-9dcb-07bacb547fb1" :step/next {:db/id 17592186425124}} {:db/id 17592186425124 :step/content {:db/id 17592186425119 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c7b7abb-15fc-5e25-af71-ce99a58976f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186425091} {:answer/id #uuid "14e7d503-39ad-5577-a641-1da1d8c70d06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "j+k" :db/id 17592186425094} {:answer/id #uuid "348a1560-eed6-553f-a07c-d5dbb0b13eae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-j+k" :db/id 17592186425098} {:answer/id #uuid "69c34c73-ac38-5363-8c2d-999f5d258274" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "j+2\,k" :db/id 17592186425103} {:answer/id #uuid "759cdd15-f659-5676-8d91-9b242c2d2b7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,j+k" :db/id 17592186425104}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186425098} :answer-field/id #uuid "9d7802a6-4174-5690-9124-8f551b3466e5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186425117}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "666541af-0f77-5a3b-95c7-e3f70c0a6b57" :question/math-academy-id "q-71228" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=3\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)-(x+y)^{3}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

"The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-2,2,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}(y-2) \\ z-1 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-3\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "dc115997-e200-5133-98f2-30e70726764f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186425123}} {:db/id 17592186425123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186425120 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fabdc74-7580-5ecf-957d-3da51c5c3bd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+k" :db/id 17592186425092} {:answer/id #uuid "1291615e-eaf6-5649-a612-304df178a8dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i+k" :db/id 17592186425093} {:answer/id #uuid "23478b53-a88f-568a-858a-7b25f93a7066" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i-2\,k" :db/id 17592186425095} {:answer/id #uuid "7733cd29-624f-51f2-ae97-a884afdbb38d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-i+k" :db/id 17592186425105} {:answer/id #uuid "e4854410-0525-5e63-82a6-354e8d687ef9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "i+2\,k" :db/id 17592186425112}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186425092} :answer-field/id #uuid "472a8778-3d0c-5974-8ff7-bc1d5d8b12f2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186425115}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d880e565-bd50-5672-98e1-45142968e59d" :question/math-academy-id "q-71226" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=5.$ Given that the point $P(4,5,-2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{\sqrt{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(4,5).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5 \\ z=x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & ={0}^{2}+{1}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1) \\  & =0+1-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-7 & =1(x) \\ z & =x+7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,7)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=x+7\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x+7$ (or $x-z+7=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it."} :step/id #uuid "c6cce728-296b-55fc-b12d-c3661e00af21"} {:db/id 17592186500430 with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a13b050c-9930-5688-bdc6-1a08f5d3cefe" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500426}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "234ff552-30db-5efc-99f4-6ca2b3ba1ac1" :answer/type {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{3} \\  & =\frac{5M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{5M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186129532 :question/id #uuid "f0af98bb-12cf-5c0f-a924-a0fe039adf99" :question/math-academy-id "q-162906"} {:db/id 17592186281631 :question/id #uuid "f8b4a4d7-db6d-5f9c-bc7b-f800dc788f58" :question/math-academy-id "q-163200"} {:db/id 17592186281632 :question/id #uuid "4167aa80-a0c6-5dcf-ad5c-868018ed4d84" :question/math-academy-id "q-163201" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "35a4e499-61e4-5d51-8488-e60716c8b89c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279063} {:answer/id #uuid "4dc2f52c-6937-5664-b1ad-a8e9f01fba53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279296} {:answer/id #uuid "77349270-7aa3-5ac9-a411-62c1c99df8b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279656} {:answer/id #uuid "81467cbe-f5a5-5724-8a67-a32eb23c17bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3M}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279753} {:answer/id #uuid "e207c367-c309-58d1-92c5-7517420bb1d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280589}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279656} :answer-field/id #uuid "5beaea88-1fc4-552a-a4a5-3b0f75db282a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280991}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[x]_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{9}\cdot 27 \\  & =3M.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}[x]_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13M}{3}.\end{aligned}

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(6-xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}6{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}y+6{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}y+6x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}16-4y+12{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[16y-2{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =48-18+108-\frac{81}{2}-0 \\  & =97.5.\end{aligned}

with mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=(x+y)\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},$ where $x$ and $y$ area measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4+\frac{8y}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[4y+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =12+12 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $y$-axis is $24\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186281621 :question/id #uuid "e47b1623-c58d-5075-9113-1251be6ca292" :question/math-academy-id "q-163170" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "257070d0-96de-5c56-8968-f3132c5ed6ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "35\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278924} {:answer/id #uuid "29c35d3d-762a-5353-98f8-756b472452d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "31\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278960} {:answer/id #uuid "9c50a528-be93-5d42-9d1d-5373833eb8d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "23.5\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279981} {:answer/id #uuid "9ec6f369-7250-5e34-b528-cb5dc49bdb12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32.4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280001} {:answer/id #uuid "eab5e69e-ea27-5171-a0d9-9069f47edb95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30.1\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186278960} :answer-field/id #uuid "cd949b6b-ce75-5adf-a47b-6ef31d9ee89f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281193}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(4y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}+4{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}36y+9+12{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[18{y}^{2}+9y+3{y}^{4}+{y}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =18+9+3+1 \\  & =31.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{4}x{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{6}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-0 \\  & =1.2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$

$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}\cdot (-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281647 :question/id #uuid "ec31a85b-303d-5111-a311-f0cb89d6a30f" :question/math-academy-id "q-163242"} {:db/id 17592186281648 :question/id #uuid "ec6fdbaa-c722-5e5b-b092-5ba93bdf0c02" :topic/math-academy-id 2027} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186130105 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130411 :tutorial/content "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively. 

![](images/b4/b4eeef756faf65e7caaf5bb8dad8d803cacf3e4f17b719868b647bf7e9c9da89.png)

Let's find the total kinetic energy of this system.

Each particle $P_i$ of mass $m_i$ has linear speed $v_i = r_i\omega.$ So, its kinetic energy is

$$
\dfrac12m_iv_i^2 = \dfrac12m_i(r_i\omega)^2 = \dfrac12m_ir_i^2\omega^2.
$$

The total kinetic energy of the system is obtained by adding the energies of all the particles. So, the kinetic energy of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total KE} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}{\omega }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the total kinetic energy of the system is given by 

$$
\text{Total KE} = \dfrac12I\omega^2,
$$

where the quantity

$$
I = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n m_ir_i^2
$$

is called the **moment of inertia** of the system about the fixed axis $L.$ The units of moment of inertia are $\rm{kg}\cdot\rm{m}^2.$

The moment of inertia in angular motion is analogous to mass in linear motion:

- For linear motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{M} v^2,
$$

where $M$ is the (total) mass of a system of particles.

The mass of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in linear motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in linear motion for a large mass than for a smaller mass.

- For angular motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{I} \omega^2,
$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of a system of particles.

The moment of inertia of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in *angular* motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in angular motion for an object with a large moment of inertia than for a body with a smaller moment of inertia." :tutorial/id #uuid Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ (in mass/area), which depends on the position.

By choosing a finite number of points $(x_{ij},y_{ij}),$ where $i=1,2,\ldots,m$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we can break the region $D$ into non-overlapping boxes $B_{ij} = [x_{ij}, x_{ij} + \Delta x] \times [y_{ij}, y_{ij} + \Delta y]$ of area $\Delta x \Delta y = \Delta A.$

![](images/c5/c5ac4166ed637b4de525f069673cc6abfaeb2e8e659b3a212d6f2f4d1bf9fc11.png)

For large $m$ and $n,$ the mass density in each box, $B_{ij}$ is approximately constant and equal to the mass density of a point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in the box. Hence, the mass of this part of the lamina is approximately the product of the mass density at this point and the area of the box:

$$
m_{ij} \approx \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \cdot \Delta A
$$

Suppose the function $r(x,y)$ gives the distance of each point $(x,y) \in D$ from a fixed axis $L.$ Then, using the formula for the moment of inertia for a collection of masses, summing over these points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{i}[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})\cdot ΔA)[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2}ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the limit as the length and width of the boxes tend to zero, we get an exact representation of the moment of inertia as an integral:

$$
I = \lim\limits_{m,n\to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^m \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) [r(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)]^2 \Delta A
= \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about a fixed axis $L$ of a plane lamina occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y)$ is

$$
I_L = \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the point $(x,y)$ to the axis $L.$

In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the $x$- and $y$-axes. Note that the distance between a point $(x,y)$ and the $x$ and $y$ coordinate axes are $r_x(x,y) = |y|$ and $r_y(x,y) = |x|,$ respectively.

![](images/8a/8a94fcdb8bb1a97e2bc9122e88ca7bd4f441299d2ce3c7bee819e644cf4eae89.png)

Hence, the moments of inertia of a plate with respect to the coordinate axes $x$ and $y,$ denoted $I_x$ and $I_y$, respectively, are 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

A related concept is the **moment of inertia about the origin** (or **polar moment of inertia**), which deals with the strength of an object when it is rotating. It is defined as

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "170c6cfe-d50a-5cee-b724-5409ca4c8461" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7794 :tutorial/title "Moment of Inertia of Plane Laminas"} :step/id #uuid "3f899894-d69b-5df5-8333-4e2b804563ee" :step/math-academy-id 45104 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130107}}] :activity/title "Moments of Inertia of Laminas About the Coordinate Axes" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129369} {:db/id 17592186130105 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130411 :tutorial/content "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively. 

![](images/b4/b4eeef756faf65e7caaf5bb8dad8d803cacf3e4f17b719868b647bf7e9c9da89.png)

Let's find the total kinetic energy of this system.

Each particle $P_i$ of mass $m_i$ has linear speed $v_i = r_i\omega.$ So, its kinetic energy is

$$
\dfrac12m_iv_i^2 = \dfrac12m_i(r_i\omega)^2 = \dfrac12m_ir_i^2\omega^2.
$$

The total kinetic energy of the system is obtained by adding the energies of all the particles. So, the kinetic energy of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total KE} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}{\omega }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the total kinetic energy of the system is given by 

$$
\text{Total KE} = \dfrac12I\omega^2,
$$

where the quantity

$$
I = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n m_ir_i^2
$$

is called the **moment of inertia** of the system about the fixed axis $L.$ The units of moment of inertia are $\rm{kg}\cdot\rm{m}^2.$

The moment of inertia in angular motion is analogous to mass in linear motion:

- For linear motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{M} v^2,
$$

where $M$ is the (total) mass of a system of particles.

The mass of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in linear motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in linear motion for a large mass than for a smaller mass.

- For angular motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{I} \omega^2,
$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of a system of particles.

The moment of inertia of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in *angular* motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in angular motion for an object with a large moment of inertia than for a body with a smaller moment of inertia." :tutorial/id #uuid "8d36ccdb-eb7d-55de-80e6-f75752dae9db" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5071 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3933d4e7-a615-5065-8581-94f59b08025e" :step/math-academy-id 31761 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130252}} {:db/id 17592186130411 :tutorial/content "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively.

If we repeat this process for moments of inertia about the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis and the origin, we obtain two more definitions. Let's summarize them below:

- The moment of inertia of ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) about ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis is given by

- The moment of inertia of ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) about ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis is given by

Note that we denote ![](images/10/10b9e6b5ce99ae6bfc544d9480ac6d62cfa9d1f23f78b8b3a331c6c517e1472d.svg) the density function expressed in polar coordinates." :tutorial/id #uuid "5d1a8a74-d440-56ad-b42b-a46e22861e20" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7766 :tutorial/title "Moments of Inertia in Polar Coordinates"} {:db/id 17592186130474 :tutorial/content "Let's now find a formula for the moment of inertia of a plane lamina with continuously varying mass density.

Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ (in mass/area), which depends on the position.

By choosing a finite number of points $(x_{ij},y_{ij}),$ where $i=1,2,\ldots,m$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we can break the region $D$ into non-overlapping boxes $B_{ij} = [x_{ij}, x_{ij} + \Delta x] \times [y_{ij}, y_{ij} + \Delta y]$ of area $\Delta x \Delta y = \Delta A.$

![](images/c5/c5ac4166ed637b4de525f069673cc6abfaeb2e8e659b3a212d6f2f4d1bf9fc11.png)

For large $m$ and $n,$ the mass density in each box, $B_{ij}$ is approximately constant and equal to the mass density of a point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in the box. Hence, the mass of this part of the lamina is approximately the product of the mass density at this point and the area of the box:

$$
m_{ij} \approx \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \cdot \Delta A
$$

Suppose the function $r(x,y)$ gives the distance of each point $(x,y) \in D$ from a fixed axis $L.$ Then, using the formula for the moment of inertia for a collection of masses, summing over these points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{i}[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})\cdot ΔA)[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2}ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the limit as the length and width of the boxes tend to zero, we get an exact representation of the moment of inertia as an integral:

$$
I = \lim\limits_{m,n\to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^m \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) [r(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)]^2 \Delta A
= \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about a fixed axis $L$ of a plane lamina occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y)$ is

$$
I_L = \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the point $(x,y)$ to the axis $L.$

In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the $x$- and $y$-axes. Note that the distance between a point $(x,y)$ and the $x$ and $y$ coordinate axes are $r_x(x,y) = |y|$ and $r_y(x,y) = |x|,$ respectively.

![](images/8a/8a94fcdb8bb1a97e2bc9122e88ca7bd4f441299d2ce3c7bee819e644cf4eae89.png)

Hence, the moments of inertia of a plate with respect to the coordinate axes $x$ and $y,$ denoted $I_x$ and $I_y$, respectively, are 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

A related concept is the **moment of inertia about the origin** (or **polar moment of inertia**), which deals with the strength of an object when it is rotating. It is defined as

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "170c6cfe-d50a-5cee-b724-5409ca4c8461" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7794 :tutorial/title "Moment of Inertia of Plane Laminas"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186435187} :activity/id #uuid "a8a272ef-3322-59e4-8457-62cd9dcd43be" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049331 :topic/id #uuid "ec6fdbaa-c722-5e5b-b092-5ba93bdf0c02" :topic/math-academy-id 2027} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186435185 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281611 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00586df5-9953-5e7a-a58f-2329aa16a468" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278586} {:answer/id #uuid "3bf84ed5-f917-50b8-8e4d-80368c472356" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279121} {:answer/id #uuid "4237198b-add2-521b-b160-d585a0924755" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279184} {:answer/id #uuid "58055d99-9594-5371-bd9f-20b8d761809d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279400} {:answer/id #uuid "86941ae5-17f0-581b-91b1-2673bcdf9949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279121} :answer-field/id #uuid "945c0f7a-70d5-5057-8a4c-71bc5f6f818a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281099}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e73bf43d-4842-564c-b994-8b4ed88b9ee2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163146" :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4+\frac{8y}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[4y+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =12+12 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}

If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=12y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 2-{y}^{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/7a/7a4216a2b1dc3859776c6589459d687981b79b123fa3a5eea638d31529e5cd3a.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}\cdot 12y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}12{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12x{y}^{3}]_{x=y}^{x=2-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12(2-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}-12{y}^{4}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}24{y}^{3}-12{y}^{5}-12{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[6{y}^{4}-2{y}^{6}-\frac{12}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6-2-\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10x.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=10r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}10r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}10{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}10{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2(32-1)(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0) \\  & =31\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f7470119-a3e9-55dd-893e-db8aec843ddb"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "104b5f45-a5a5-53b8-81f3-1afa7e730667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "23" "c204945d-1cc7-5037-a46b-3df54b66b209" :question/math-academy-id "q-163183" :question/problem "![](images/dc/dc61efd6e5ef1fd46fca53f7c1e47394c6b9c95fb2455dc0c798d9936a68631b.png)

A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the $x$-axis, $y$-axis, and the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/62/626cbf8e182d9eebb8b48026f07c5dd012c1096cc9568465f3648710ea0d07a4.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(10y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}10{x}^{2}y+10{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})+\frac{5}{2}{(4-{x}^{2})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{2}(4-{x}^{2})(2{x}^{2}+4-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}16-{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[16x-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(32-\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8cc8c4c3-672d-51c1-af40-2419b51ec4f9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442861}} {:db/id 17592186442858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281633 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c84deba-cb38-5f3b-af0e-58521ec502a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279280} {:answer/id #uuid "a25defa0-44b9-5bda-a10f-e6ef6a677aaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280035} {:answer/id #uuid "ad5bf3b6-9c4b-50ce-879e-8ec79739fdf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280127} {:answer/id #uuid "ca352098-298f-5e14-a7d7-0c7272084e0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280364} {:answer/id #uuid "cf1d4484-aff6-5376-8a09-a8cd9f6af638" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280418}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280127} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a384dc8-494e-5973-bebc-5b4d13e8a8c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "095d8c09-ff9b-5528-8c3d-3967d18698a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163204" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{[\frac{8y}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "9a68fb24-0279-5aa2-9378-bef9856a349d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442859}} {:db/id 17592186442859 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281642 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17226919-ce93-5049-994f-31d7cd5c10fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186278798} {:answer/id #uuid "6d3b17cc-de83-57bb-914f-013137289a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186279586} {:answer/id #uuid "78cff65f-0d69-5e60-9e1c-47253821dc1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186279669} {:answer/id #uuid "8d83c82c-bb2f-532f-ab7d-a58f6e2cc4be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186279853} {:answer/id #uuid "e875a915-69ff-5a94-9c30-f7fd03b5fb84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{10}" :db/id 17592186280639}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279586} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf0fe541-fc86-58e2-a9d5-645ba6b20816" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281172}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2726afac-54d3-5734-a6e0-8fa5ce77d367" :question/math-academy-id "q-163228" :question/problem "![](images/04/044395de3b30755d0c83d489709c38420827f6984af740bc56a3dc5bfaa33794.png)

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{[\frac{8y}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\,{|}_{2}^{3}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(9-4)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}

Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{2}\cdot x{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{3}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{2y}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}60{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[30{e}^{2y}]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =120-30 \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
