Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "63d1ac8f-1120-57bf-a3f2-068394de0e68" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481469}} {:db/id 17592186481456 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281644 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24eeb6dc-6a62-5d90-a207-0acfc7258433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186278919} {:answer/id #uuid "349f0582-d339-5e4d-9545-b31c93cda4da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}-1" :db/id 17592186279045} {:answer/id #uuid "538264a8-2746-5c22-950d-ad36b0c19129" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}" :db/id 17592186279351} {:answer/id #uuid "c7b8065a-0247-55f8-99df-fad5f0147068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280342} {:answer/id #uuid "f2ebd0da-d30a-58a4-863a-0db44212f7d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186280710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279351} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec2db863-9898-51d6-ba39-8b881e966e18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281253}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b6b312d9-6efa-541f-ad5d-be93b575260c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163230" :question/problem "![](images/ad/ad7c939aded3f5e5e1e2f3b5e5743609e331625479c25f6a55659be730ed1cf5.png)

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=15y.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}\cdot (-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6cb00066-5889-5430-a707-e706993fe08c"} {:db/id 17592186481462 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281622 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e774e3e-5483-570a-be90-3556fdfeef80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96" :db/id 17592186278875} {:answer/id #uuid "264c43c5-9ce5-5021-829e-191395085650" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "66" :db/id 17592186278931} {:answer/id #uuid "27a3b396-361a-5015-9461-0aae23b48259" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "88" :db/id 17592186278947} {:answer/id #uuid "4373458f-0c28-5ba9-9faf-49c7a51e957d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "124" :db/id 17592186279197} {:answer/id #uuid "aec868ad-08a2-517d-b508-f8953c729333" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "112" :db/id 17592186280137}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280137} :answer-field/id #uuid "13ebe4cc-aac8-5388-84d5-8872f110619f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280865}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "566286c6-ab64-5382-ab24-0d1952795e00" :question/math-academy-id "q-163174" :question/problem "![](images/a6/a6910defd242e1b65b7bdf8b580cd2f56df3ac43951a9f83f353003e00a849b4.png)

$$

$$

$$

A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the lines $y=0$, $x=4$, and the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=3y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/dd/dd5ee021dd73317a775c0ea653212f7ee5545f8c6854e6a9daabdc93b5c3b9c0.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 3y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =96+16 \\  & =112.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9a3dcded-2a78-5806-a252-b52ade3817a0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481453}} {:db/id 17592186481453 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281636 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3d50eaec-2761-511b-a299-ac2ff1333565" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{3}" :db/id 17592186279131} {:answer/id #uuid "68823909-c88a-5645-9191-b732f12dac1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3M" :db/id 17592186279542} {:answer/id #uuid "79aa1e53-51b6-5bde-8f08-eb601cf1e05f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{2}" :db/id 17592186279676} {:answer/id #uuid "856764d8-02ae-52b0-88dd-114d96718896" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M" :db/id 17592186279789} {:answer/id #uuid "cf88cb2f-c430-5ef6-8cc7-c99324e16f93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3M}{2}" :db/id 17592186280419}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280419} :answer-field/id #uuid "adf88e2d-a46f-5e96-b3db-c6aa9b189759" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281131}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "96817e72-a430-5366-920a-3988e4d8fc65" :question/math-academy-id "q-163217" :question/problem "![](images/de/de3753a45554be28283e74116510ff6c3b67560fce79d1570c819a215f6e10f3.png)

A triangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the $x$-axis and the lines $y=3x$ and $y=4-x,$ as shown above. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "63d1ac8f-1120-57bf-a3f2-068394de0e68" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481469}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3d50eaec-2761-511b-a299-ac2ff1333565" :answer/type {:db/id A triangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the $y$-axis and the lines $y=\frac{x}{2}$ and $y=3-x,$ as shown above. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le 3-x\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/6c/6c2cec5e919c25623396b5ba5f052481623a868c7520aa8e3d1d3eb34f3a4a58.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 3=3.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(3-x-\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(8-6) \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "de27f7da-aa86-5902-bdef-f289c3a397f0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481456}} {:db/id 17592186481456 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281644 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24eeb6dc-6a62-5d90-a207-0acfc7258433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186278919} {:answer/id #uuid "349f0582-d339-5e4d-9545-b31c93cda4da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}-1" :db/id 17592186279045} {:answer/id #uuid "538264a8-2746-5c22-950d-ad36b0c19129" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}" :db/id 17592186279351} {:answer/id #uuid "c7b8065a-0247-55f8-99df-fad5f0147068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280342} {:answer/id #uuid "f2ebd0da-d30a-58a4-863a-0db44212f7d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186280710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279351} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec2db863-9898-51d6-ba39-8b881e966e18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281253}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b6b312d9-6efa-541f-ad5d-be93b575260c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163230" :question/problem "![](images/ad/ad7c939aded3f5e5e1e2f3b5e5743609e331625479c25f6a55659be730ed1cf5.png)

Consider the plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=\sqrt[5]{2}$ and the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=15y.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}\cdot (-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6cb00066-5889-5430-a707-e706993fe08c"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24eeb6dc-6a62-5d90-a207-0acfc7258433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326394}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =-2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(12+6)-1(-4-0) \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}.\end{aligned}

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=x,\,v(x,y,z)=z-y,\,w(x,y,z)=xy.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ y & x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ x & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(0-x) \\  & =-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x & =-u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281336 :question/id #uuid "9bd3e29c-50b2-5640-b3fa-d0adf89e1fac" :question/math-academy-id "q-161806" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21988933-2fdd-5343-979b-14ba2f6e68d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{uvw}}" :db/id 17592186278894} {:answer/id #uuid "413d8651-c816-595c-bfd1-f51fa29900be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}" :db/id 17592186279172} {:answer/id #uuid "4e964f3b-c23d-5355-8277-f886ef034e49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{uvw}" :db/id 17592186279306} {:answer/id #uuid "7bc53c83-70d3-5bd8-adc4-31458e829c60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4uvw" :db/id 17592186279694} {:answer/id #uuid "8888de73-401c-58c0-8c74-d084f5008000" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{uvw}" :db/id 17592186279811}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279172} :answer-field/id #uuid "efb87408-7532-5806-bc11-5c1c98d338e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281257}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}

$$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z\ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}\begin{vmatrix}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{vmatrix}+2yz\begin{vmatrix}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424181 :question/id #uuid "bbf87425-cede-5e7e-870f-278bd2b11904" :question/math-academy-id "q-161808" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129269 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e290e8b2-7766-55ff-95da-99a3430b18e3" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of an Inverse Transformation"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ba467583-3a17-5baa-8344-2ff452a1d080" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{u}" :db/id 17592186424165} {:answer/id #uuid "bc7a65b8-5911-5995-890e-26eb26de2d86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4}{vw}" :db/id 17592186424166} {:answer/id #uuid "cda476b6-e024-5c13-a813-a0217e4446ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{v}{{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186424167} {:answer/id #uuid "ecf34300-0330-5f0e-9e12-24a74c4b83db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2u}{v-w}" :db/id 17592186424170} {:answer/id #uuid "fa885cf6-9f29-528c-8aeb-86e960fc0083" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{w}{v}" :db/id 17592186424172}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ba467583-3a17-5baa-8344-2ff452a1d080" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{u}" :db/id 17592186424165} :answer-field/id #uuid "f602c505-c9b2-58a6-873a-3101dc02439a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186424177}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{z}{y} \\ y \\ xz\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $y,z\ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{y},\,v(x,y,z)=y,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{z}{{y}^{2}} & \frac{1}{y} \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =z(0-\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =-\frac{z}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{z}{y} & =-u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-u)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186424182 :question/id #uuid "fa96e0b4-9142-5b9e-b173-68571a2c2de3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161797" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0584ff70-04f9-53f4-b918-d40c95661794" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186424148} {:answer/id #uuid "274585a0-b8c0-5396-9ba1-f844d74ca493" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186424151} {:answer/id #uuid "2dad3fa0-8b4c-595d-a450-31167f619d29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186424152} {:answer/id #uuid "d83940ba-986b-5a11-adf3-d93e8cc8e5b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186424168} {:answer/id #uuid "f587a66a-7aeb-56f0-8880-52bcb09867b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186424171}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424168} :answer-field/id #uuid "b9faf9fb-252c-510a-b14d-4675e0404650" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424175}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129270 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128847 :question/id #uuid "b16845a2-5f66-524a-90ea-37f8a8186f8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-11518"} :knowledge-point/id "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186402682}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}-v \\ {u}^{2}+v \\ {e}^{w}\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186281338 :question/id #uuid "d47d2404-bd86-5706-ba43-4f015172617a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161809" $$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u \\ {v}^{3}+{w}^{3} \\ v+w\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)={v}^{3}+{w}^{3},\,z(u,v,w)=v+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =3{w}^{2} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(3{v}^{2}-3{w}^{2}) \\  & =3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}) & =0 \\ {v}^{2}-{w}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation ${v}^{2}-{w}^{2}=0$ defines a pair of intersecting planes $v=w$ and $v=-w.$"} {:db/id 17592186281340 :question/id #uuid "e2d2dfd0-abce-5610-a53e-633420f43575" :question/math-academy-id $$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u}+v,\,y(u,v,w)=v+w,\,z(u,v,w)=vw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}(v-w).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ {e}^{u}(v-w) & =0 \\ v-w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v-w=0$ defines the plane $v=w.$"} {:db/id 17592186129271 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128848 :question/id #uuid "66d757d2-f2ad-5f0d-b4f1-8d426f4c8351" :step/math-academy-id 42966 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130210}} {:db/id 17592186130212 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d8ced6e6-4bb6-52e9-8819-7a54180e8a4f" :step/math-academy-id 43046 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130234}} {:db/id 17592186130213 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129271 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128848 :question/id #uuid "66d757d2-f2ad-5f0d-b4f1-8d426f4c8351" :question/math-academy-id "e-11579"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d433063f-f145-5bf4-8bd4-8d5e5b36b3d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048219} {:db/id 17592186048505} {:db/id 17592186049159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129727} {:db/id 17592186129750} {:db/id 17592186281325} {:db/id 17592186281326} {:db/id 17592186281327} {:db/id 17592186281328} {:db/id 17592186406772} {:db/id 17592186424178} {:db/id 17592186424179} {:db/id 17592186510378} {:db/id 17592186510461}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "d3c03e1b-973d-566a-96d2-32f746decf45" :step/math-academy-id 43048 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130229}} {:db/id 17592186130229 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130463 :tutorial/content "The **critical points** of a transformation $\mathbf T: \mathbb R^3\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$ given by

![](images/0f/0f47dfd79a5147b5628975b26ea21a37288d809fb30a5a90b205ecc7b25ae008.svg)

are the points in Cartesian $uvw$-space where the Jacobian is zero:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}=0
$$

  

Similar to the two-dimensional case, the transformation $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible at the critical points.

Finally, provided that $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, the connection between the Jacobians of $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right)^{-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9dd5b9bc-94c3-5fd0-8752-3fa9be521934" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7676 :tutorial/title "The Critical Points of a Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "99520515-6bfa-5265-8e42-e193dc1183f6" :step/math-academy-id 44587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130211}} {:db/id 17592186130234 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130467 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant of a spatial transformation can be interpreted similarly to the Jacobian of a plane transformation.

As before, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

Given that $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ denotes the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0, w_0),$ let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space whose bottom, back left corner is at the point $(u_0,v_0,w_0).$

![](images/31/31c0a7275acdac0dc217e73f3c1e3d9efe504832419c87486cee980e20ea04da.png)

 

It can be shown that, provided that our prism is very small and $(u_0,v_0, w_0)$ is not a critical point of $\mathbf T,$ the image of our prism can be approximated by a parallelepiped. 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangular prism and its (approximate) image:

- The local *volume* scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length, width, and height of our rectangular prism are $\delta u,$ $\delta v,$ and $\delta w,$ so its volume is 

$$
\delta V = \delta u \delta v \delta w.
$$

 Then, it can be shown that the approximate parallelepiped in $xyz$-space has a volume equal to 

$$
\left|J(u_0,v_0,w_0)\right| \cdot \delta V,
$$

 as depicted below.

![](images/d6/d669cd5369d33e618ab43cfd3e93ee70c9fea8420b5a829d78826c11524511aa.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) > 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving. 

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the same orientation (right-handed $\to$ right-handed or left-handed $\to$ left-handed).

![](images/f0/f05f9a79d9156518e948c46f6c67eb5ff31132fd4a088e14219eada7eb49a441.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0, w_0) < 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the opposite orientation (right-handed $\to$ left-handed or left-handed $\to$ right-handed).

![](images/45/45b08e0fec7114db52a05cb42ed46d7d62baa5b01a5dea37752928348802b205.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) \neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a three-dimensional region (i.e., a parallelepiped).

![](images/61/61557eb2d78d468946375b918ab182da518b7cf2c68a1c0a0593c93b991bcf78.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a two-dimensional region (a parallelogram), a one-dimensional region (a line segment), or a zero-dimensional region (a point).

![](images/72/726ba518de982ddd0b2924a645463b496ed881ead76a652c812c7a164aa684b8.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "10a3ad60-7124-5508-a053-b827183f5a2a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7718 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "ed9fa5db-a7c0-512a-bb14-c0e7e5dcbcd0" :step/math-academy-id 44764 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130213}}] :activity/title "The Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129388} {:db/id 17592186130212 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title :step/math-academy-id 42966 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130210}} {:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130234 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130467 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant of a spatial transformation can be interpreted similarly to the Jacobian of a plane transformation.

As before, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

Given that $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ denotes the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0, w_0),$ let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space whose bottom, back left corner is at the point $(u_0,v_0,w_0).$

![](images/31/31c0a7275acdac0dc217e73f3c1e3d9efe504832419c87486cee980e20ea04da.png)

 

It can be shown that, provided that our prism is very small and $(u_0,v_0, w_0)$ is not a critical point of $\mathbf T,$ the image of our prism can be approximated by a parallelepiped. 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangular prism and its (approximate) image:

- The local *volume* scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length, width, and height of our rectangular prism are $\delta u,$ $\delta v,$ and $\delta w,$ so its volume is 

$$
\delta V = \delta u \delta v \delta w.
$$

 Then, it can be shown that the approximate parallelepiped in $xyz$-space has a volume equal to 

$$
\left|J(u_0,v_0,w_0)\right| \cdot \delta V,
$$

 as depicted below.

![](images/d6/d669cd5369d33e618ab43cfd3e93ee70c9fea8420b5a829d78826c11524511aa.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) > 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving. 

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the same orientation (right-handed $\to$ right-handed or left-handed $\to$ left-handed).

![](images/f0/f05f9a79d9156518e948c46f6c67eb5ff31132fd4a088e14219eada7eb49a441.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0, w_0) < 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the opposite orientation (right-handed $\to$ left-handed or left-handed $\to$ right-handed).

![](images/45/45b08e0fec7114db52a05cb42ed46d7d62baa5b01a5dea37752928348802b205.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) \neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a three-dimensional region (i.e., a parallelepiped).

![](images/61/61557eb2d78d468946375b918ab182da518b7cf2c68a1c0a0593c93b991bcf78.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a two-dimensional region (a parallelogram), a one-dimensional region (a line segment), or a zero-dimensional region (a point).

![](images/72/726ba518de982ddd0b2924a645463b496ed881ead76a652c812c7a164aa684b8.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "10a3ad60-7124-5508-a053-b827183f5a2a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7718 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "ed9fa5db-a7c0-512a-bb14-c0e7e5dcbcd0" :step/math-academy-id 44764 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130213}} {:db/id 17592186130213 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129271 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128848 :question/id #uuid "66d757d2-f2ad-5f0d-b4f1-8d426f4c8351" :question/math-academy-id "e-11579"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d433063f-f145-5bf4-8bd4-8d5e5b36b3d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048219} {:db/id 17592186048505} {:db/id 17592186049159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129727} {:db/id 17592186129750} {:db/id 17592186281325} {:db/id 17592186281326} {:db/id 17592186281327} {:db/id 17592186281328} {:db/id 17592186406772} {:db/id 17592186424178} {:db/id 17592186424179} {:db/id 17592186510378} {:db/id 17592186510461}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "d3c03e1b-973d-566a-96d2-32f746decf45" :step/math-academy-id 43048 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130229}} {:db/id 17592186130229 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130463 :tutorial/content "The **critical points** of a transformation $\mathbf T: \mathbb R^3\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$ given by

![](images/0f/0f47dfd79a5147b5628975b26ea21a37288d809fb30a5a90b205ecc7b25ae008.svg)

are the points in Cartesian $uvw$-space where the Jacobian is zero:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}=0
$$

  

Similar to the two-dimensional case, the transformation $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible at the critical points.

Finally, provided that $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, the connection between the Jacobians of $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is as follows:

\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right)^{-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9dd5b9bc-94c3-5fd0-8752-3fa9be521934" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7676 :tutorial/title "The Critical Points of a Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "99520515-6bfa-5265-8e42-e193dc1183f6" :step/math-academy-id 44587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130211}} {:db/id 17592186130463 :tutorial/content "The **critical points** of a transformation $\mathbf T: \mathbb R^3\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$ given by

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ab44c8de-700d-51cc-ab4a-3755f7926aef" :question/math-academy-id "q-39709" :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}{u}^{2}-v \\ {u}^{2}+v \\ {e}^{w}\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}\begin{vmatrix}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "1059b764-2977-50ff-bfe0-2e03c6d8a3b7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186416649}} {:db/id 17592186416648 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129728 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "408e29c9-6522-5467-9ab8-def9fe8cfb65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{{u}^{2}}{2\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186324490} {:answer/id #uuid "69224e59-e1c5-54cd-8748-b2d597b5cd76" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{w}{u}^{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186324848} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1e869c-a3b7-584b-8e0f-e99423947eb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{u}^{2}}{2\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186325004} {:answer/id #uuid "e98f16dc-8225-5762-aa80-dca5e80b6645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186326027} {:answer/id #uuid "fb5ec600-18ee-54e3-bb28-7c22c6783223" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}" :db/id 17592186326182}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326027} :answer-field/id #uuid "65802821-8118-5ece-8435-a69816ad88f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326394}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f85af4c0-4520-5614-952b-cb9d6d06c6c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-39300" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}

#uuid "9bd3e29c-50b2-5640-b3fa-d0adf89e1fac" :question/math-academy-id "q-161806" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}xy \\ yz \\ xz\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "363a88a5-6e96-5462-af6d-738ef0ce316a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488312}} {:db/id 17592186488312 :step/content {:db/id 17592186424180 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e37282e-8869-5ad2-9f01-e062a7d21846" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the parabolic cylinder $v=2{w}^{2}.$" :db/id 17592186424153} {:answer/id #uuid "4a31e95b-7336-5699-a485-0b22a7563452" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the plane $v=w.$" :db/id 17592186424154} {:answer/id #uuid "56201c08-96c0-58d8-9ed7-c9a2a6ecea11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the $vw-$plane." :db/id 17592186424156} {:answer/id #uuid "7447254c-742a-5c7f-adb1-193a3168832a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the $uv-$plane." :db/id 17592186424159} {:answer/id #uuid "7473d403-04c8-5521-92cd-20ba6d10f904" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The critical points lie on the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4.$" :db/id 17592186424160}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424154} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0a37030-5cd9-5e43-a291-e19dfc94c67f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424176}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b50230b8-d517-560a-9ede-747bedde3c3c" :question/math-academy-id "q-161811" :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}

Here, we have 

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =1 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =v\end{aligned}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}{e}^{u} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ w & v\end{vmatrix} \\  & ={e}^{u}(v-w).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ {e}^{u}(v-w) & =0 \\ v-w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)={v}^{3}+{w}^{3},\,z(u,v,w)=v+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =3{w}^{2} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(3{v}^{2}-3{w}^{2}) \\  & =3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}) & =0 \\ {v}^{2}-{w}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation ${v}^{2}-{w}^{2}=0$ defines a pair of intersecting planes $v=w$ and $v=-w.$"} :step/id #uuid "f60d8ef1-6b2a-5dbe-9e22-142cc6c61acf"}] :activity/title "The Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186487563} {:db/id 17592186488324 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129751 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a3dfa61-4983-5101-a590-b7cae3069606" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186324062} {:answer/id #uuid "5975b6e2-4d63-5522-bc15-85311b4304c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186324714} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d3c1d8-1ca4-5893-ae40-8a4995898733" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{16}" :db/id 17592186325383} {:answer/id #uuid "c5fd3b47-8f20-518a-a996-2dbd4fa2edc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{40}" :db/id 17592186325679} {:answer/id #uuid "fcb623d2-5638-5465-9671-82a386df23f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "40" :db/id 17592186326195}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325679} :answer-field/id #uuid "5d44cd8a-7ab2-5c59-a740-4c19610ad44c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326377}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9ad6bc33-7c9a-5d03-8204-18b81f486eea" :question/math-academy-id "q-39669" :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=-x+3y-2z,\,w=3y+4z.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =-2 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =3 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(12+6)-1(-4-0) \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9dc9075-d2e1-5d44-af9c-c5a92178e242" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488335}} {:db/id 17592186488299 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281336 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21988933-2fdd-5343-979b-14ba2f6e68d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{uvw}}" :db/id 17592186278894} {:answer/id #uuid "413d8651-c816-595c-bfd1-f51fa29900be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}" :db/id 17592186279172} {:answer/id #uuid "4e964f3b-c23d-5355-8277-f886ef034e49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{uvw}" :db/id 17592186279306} {:answer/id #uuid "7bc53c83-70d3-5bd8-adc4-31458e829c60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4uvw" :db/id 17592186279694} {:answer/id #uuid "8888de73-401c-58c0-8c74-d084f5008000" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{uvw}" :db/id 17592186279811}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279172} :answer-field/id #uuid "efb87408-7532-5806-bc11-5c1c98d338e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281257}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9bd3e29c-50b2-5640-b3fa-d0adf89e1fac" :question/math-academy-id "q-161806" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by
