{T}^{-1}:\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}xy \\ yz \\ xz\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=xy,\,v(x,y,z)=yz,\,w(x,y,z)=xz.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =z & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =y \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =z & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}y & x & 0 \\ 0 & z & y \\ z & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y\begin{vmatrix}z & y \\ 0 & x\end{vmatrix}-x\begin{vmatrix}0 & y \\ z & x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =y(xz-0)-x(0-yz) \\  & =xyz+xyz \\  & =2xyz.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz & =2\sqrt{(xyz)^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{xy(yz)(xz)} \\  & =2\sqrt{uvw}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{uvw}}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "363a88a5-6e96-5462-af6d-738ef0ce316a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488312}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "21988933-2fdd-5343-979b-14ba2f6e68d4" :answer/type {:db/id "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}⟶\begin{bmatrix}u \\ {v}^{3}+{w}^{3} \\ v+w\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u,\,y(u,v,w)={v}^{3}+{w}^{3},\,z(u,v,w)=v+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =3{v}^{2} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =3{w}^{2} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}3{v}^{2} & 3{w}^{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(3{v}^{2}-3{w}^{2}) \\  & =3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 3({v}^{2}-{w}^{2}) & =0 \\ {v}^{2}-{w}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation ${v}^{2}-{w}^{2}=0$ defines a pair of intersecting planes $v=w$ and $v=-w.$"} :step/id #uuid "f60d8ef1-6b2a-5dbe-9e22-142cc6c61acf"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fa96e0b4-9142-5b9e-b173-68571a2c2de3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161797" :question/problem "Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)),$ given that 

$$
u=x,\,v=2y,\,w=3z.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v \\ w\end{bmatrix}\to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{bmatrix},
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(6-0) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ce86c9dd-b527-5f1d-96bb-d695b6d536b3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186488299}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0584ff70-04f9-53f4-b918-d40c95661794" :answer/type {:db/id $$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. Less than half of Lionel's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

II. More than half of David's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

III. Lionel had a greater percentage of goals scored from the penalty spot compared to David.

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
12%<50%,
$$

less than half of Lionel's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

- Statement II is false. Notice that 

$$
0.1<0.5.
$$

So, less than half of David's goals scored were from the penalty spot.

- Statement III is true. We can compare $12%$ and $0.1$ by converting the decimal into a percent. 

To do this, we multiply it by $100:$

$$
0.1\times 100=10%
$$

Since  $12%>10%,$ Lionel had a **greater** percentage of goals scored from the penalty spot compared to David.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."} {:db/id 17592186147802 :question/id #uuid "f2cc0d53-2a89-5a27-98eb-885f1d459e75" :question/math-academy-id "q-350257"} {:db/id 17592186434388 :question/id #uuid "16a4ed86-6ba4-5b08-b5bc-00c64da3da49" :question/math-academy-id "q-350266" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "825bb7d0-2dd7-5898-b09d-fa36c3af945c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453868} {:answer/id #uuid "b7ee75e3-c277-58e5-8016-0f292274075f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453869}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453869} :answer-field/id #uuid "27377df2-4049-5654-9b05-2bd96fc9143a" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454684} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ffa5102c-c608-5436-b9c9-a71c559e2def" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453870} {:answer/id #uuid "c3c895d9-44a3-52c0-ab7d-3d644c95fa8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453871}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453870} :answer-field/id #uuid "90d78070-dbec-5fd0-85ce-332d66270d76" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454685} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cac6f298-f93a-5381-8ee2-f655b4a4bb52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186453872} {:answer/id #uuid "91b100af-367e-5f51-bd41-32339c196cd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186453873}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186453872} :answer-field/id #uuid "08559b28-05c3-5429-8dcc-9459d6dd6efb" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186454686}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Sana and Talia are students. :tutorial/content "We can find **equivalent ratios** by multiplying or dividing all numbers in a ratio by the same value. 

To demonstrate, let's consider the following ratio:

$$
2:6
$$

If we multiply *both* numbers by $5,$ for example, we get the ratio $10:30.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓\times \,5 &  &  &  & \,\,↓\times \,5 &  \\ \,10 &  & : &  & \,30 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratios $2:6$ and $10:30$ are equivalent. 

Similarly, if we take the ratio $2:6$ and divide *both* numbers by $2,$ we get $1:3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,2 &  &  &  & \,\,↓÷\,2 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,3 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratios  $2:6$ and  $1:3$ are also equivalent." :tutorial/id #uuid "cc2c9ce9-c2b0-5d68-81db-b8b0273407f0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8203 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6aa20fa4-3163-5025-84f7-a1ddd4324cd0" :step/math-academy-id 186681 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074635}} {:db/id 17592186074635 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075035 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the following two ratios are equivalent:

What is the missing number?

To find a ratio equivalent to $3 : 5,$ we multiply or divide both numbers by the same value. 

In this case, we need to get $12$ from ${\color{blue}{3}},$ so we multiply ${\color{blue}{3}}$ by $4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,3 &  & : & \,\,\, & \,\,5 &  \\ \,\,↓\times \,4 &  &  &  & \,\,↓\times \,4 &  \\ 12 &  & : &  & \,\boxed{\text{[math]\phantom{0}[/math]}} & \end{aligned}
$$

So, to get ![](images/50/50f3c1b8dc3b1628130d1de11abcc455fc22006f32b7486f658c8134fcc3221c.svg) from ${\color{red}{5}},$ we multiply ${\color{red}{5}}$ by $4$ as well: 

$$
{\color{red}5} \times 4 = \bbox[3px,lightgray]{\color{red}20}
$$

Therefore, the missing number is $20.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3539d419-9d5a-5467-8a88-7ef318329859" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8204 :tutorial/title "Finding Missing Values in Equivalent Ratios"} :step/id #uuid "4854b84c-59a0-5a98-a9c6-9b8427de8ab8" :step/math-academy-id 186682 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074636}} {:db/id 17592186074636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186073738 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186073447 :question/id #uuid "a453e80d-016f-5a6c-9890-705463eb1fb9" :question/math-academy-id "e-13120"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f3ac1e54-c949-5ffe-b377-b0e35240a13c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048351} {:db/id 17592186050924}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186074085} {:db/id 17592186074388} {:db/id 17592186434315} {:db/id 17592186434316}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Equivalent Ratios"} :step/id #uuid "55be2711-44d0-588a-899f-562ac0853236" :step/math-academy-id 186683 :step/next {:db/id 17592186074637}} {:db/id 17592186074637 :step/content {:db/id 17592186075036 :tutorial/content "We can simplify ratios by dividing both numbers in the ratio by a common factor.

$$

$$

The numbers $18$ and $9$ share a common factor of $9,$ so we can divide both numbers by $9$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,18 &  & : & \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,9 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,\,9 &  &  &  & \,\,\,↓÷\,\,9 &  \\ \,\,2 &  & : &  & \,\,\,1 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $18:9$ is equivalent to $2:1.$

What ratio describes the number of triangles to the number of pentagons?" :question/worked-solution "We count the number of triangles. We see that there are $2$ triangles.

We count the number of pentagons. We see that there are $4$ pentagons.

So the ratio of triangles to pentagons is $2:4.$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing both numbers in a ratio by $2:$

$$

:tutorial/content "When we subtract a positive number from another positive number, we move towards the left on the number line. 

For example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
3 - 5
$$

To subtract $5$ from $3,$ we start at $3$ on the number line and move $5$ places to the left.

![](images/57/57ac1fe7a28ae5fefadf900d2276d499cdccf01df48b819b0aafa5347a2ec506.png)

When we do this, we land at $-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
3-5 = -2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8af27dde-6aa4-5067-84f8-9538f1acaa18" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8029 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e99d8d22-f103-5560-a608-35f0957133f4" :step/math-academy-id 188374 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065132}} {:db/id 17592186065132 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064255 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063935 :question/id #uuid "34280e7c-023c-5c7f-b22b-3f322ff97dad" :question/math-academy-id "e-12813"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6a3c970b-4086-52ef-ac0f-2b8c3d72fd51" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049429}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064527} {:db/id 17592186064570} {:db/id 17592186064629} {:db/id 17592186433314} {:db/id 17592186433317} {:db/id 17592186433318} {:db/id 17592186433319} {:db/id 17592186433320}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting a Positive Number From a Non-Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "a7e8a41f-1f30-5c54-b22b-c51e7a5efd82" :step/math-academy-id 188375 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065133}} {:db/id 17592186065133 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065413 :tutorial/content "It is impractical to use number lines to subtract large numbers. 

However, a neat trick makes subtracting a positive number from a smaller positive number very easy!

As an example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}}
$$

Since $68$ is larger than $37,$ the answer *must be negative*.

We start by solving an easier problem: subtracting the numbers *in the reverse order*. In our case, the reverse problem is

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}}.
$$

Next, we carry out the subtraction:

![](images/db/db192e5c1f089e3d4cc2a7b1238392e44a7ba36bff99345a997042c16ebc304f.svg)

So, we have

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}} = 31.
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}} = -31.
$$

And that's it! 

Let's use the same idea to subtract two three-digit numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "d7dbb60e-47d5-56db-981a-145c532f7ace" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8030 :tutorial/title "Subtraction With Larger Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "12b96179-bf32-5136-bbf1-e7631a656dfb" :step/math-academy-id 188379 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065134}} {:db/id 17592186065134 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064256 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063936 :question/id #uuid "1850f823-4159-5bd1-afac-71d8090c754b" :question/math-academy-id "e-12814"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f1c51da0-7569-50c0-b405-c74419d47ef3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049516}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064485} {:db/id 17592186064526} {:db/id 17592186064528} {:db/id 17592186433315} {:db/id 17592186433316} {:db/id 17592186433321} {:db/id 17592186433322}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting a Positive Number From a Non-Negative Number With Larger Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "9f2475d1-01ac-524a-9a5e-a1adfdc797a2" :step/math-academy-id 188380}] :activity/title "Subtracting a Positive Number From a Smaller Positive Number" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064418} {:db/id 17592186065131 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065412 :tutorial/content "When we subtract a positive number from another positive number, we move towards the left on the number line.

However, a neat trick makes subtracting a positive number from a smaller positive number very easy!

As an example, let's consider the following subtraction problem:

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}}
$$

Since $68$ is larger than $37,$ the answer *must be negative*.

We start by solving an easier problem: subtracting the numbers *in the reverse order*. In our case, the reverse problem is

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}}.
$$

Next, we carry out the subtraction:

![](images/db/db192e5c1f089e3d4cc2a7b1238392e44a7ba36bff99345a997042c16ebc304f.svg)

So, we have

$$
{\color{blue}{68}} - {\color{red}{37}} = 31.
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{\color{red}{37}} - {\color{blue}{68}} = -31.
$$

And that's it! 

Let's use the same idea to subtract two three-digit numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "d7dbb60e-47d5-56db-981a-145c532f7ace" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8030 :tutorial/title "Subtraction With Larger Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "12b96179-bf32-5136-bbf1-e7631a656dfb" :step/math-academy-id 188379 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065134}} {:db/id 17592186065413 :tutorial/content "It is impractical to use number lines to subtract large numbers.

:topic/math-academy-id 2457} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186148482 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148698 :tutorial/content "When working with fractions, percents, and decimals, we often need to decide which number is greater or smaller. Since these numbers are written in different forms, it can be difficult to compare them directly.

To make comparisons easier, we can *convert them to a common form*.

For example, let's compare the percent $48\%$ and the decimal $0.52$.

One way to do that is to convert the percent to a decimal. So, we divide the percent value by $100{:}$

$$
48 \div 100 = 0.48
$$

Thus, $48\%$ is equivalent to $0.48$.

Now, we can compare the two decimals:
$0.48 < 0.52$

Therefore, we can conclude that $48\%$ is smaller than $0.52$.

Let's see more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "e6681afa-a432-5074-a46c-204561f2cf65" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2078 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d9c7592c-10c0-5cc3-b1ff-b5b67dfe08ba" :step/math-academy-id 632742 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148483}} {:db/id 17592186148483 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147542 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147245 :question/id #uuid "7dd3b106-ac45-522a-97ea-6dc4355f0247" :question/math-academy-id "e-2317"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6be40082-db16-5983-aa43-9b6ee8f59def" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049298} {:db/id 17592186050030}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147795} {:db/id 17592186147796}] :knowledge-point/title "Comparing a Decimal to a Percent"} :step/id #uuid "5df02fb6-3576-5996-8b1e-64978fa7b5d8" :step/math-academy-id 632743 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148484}} {:db/id 17592186148484 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147543 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147246 :question/id #uuid "22bfefb3-89b4-5d42-b305-732790c89fbd" :question/math-academy-id "e-2318"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "37060efd-560b-5d57-b108-07c202e3abcc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049640} {:db/id 17592186050478}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147797} {:db/id 17592186147798} {:db/id 17592186434387}] :knowledge-point/title "Comparing a Percent to a Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "f6835341-5e27-57e3-ae67-a97b6df1ba75" :step/math-academy-id 632746 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148485}} {:db/id 17592186148485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148670 :tutorial/content "Suppose Ethan and Ryan are baseball players. In the previous season, $24\%$ of Ethan’s hits were home runs, while the decimal proportion of Ryan’s hits that were home runs was $0.3$.

Let’s determine whether either Ethan or Ryan hit home runs on more than half of their total hits.

- *For Ethan*, we compare his statistic to one-half written as a percentage, $50\%$. Since
$24\% < 50\%$,
less than half of Ethan’s hits were home runs.
- *For Ryan*, we compare his statistic to one-half written as a decimal, $0.5$. Since
$0.3 < 0.5$,
less than half of Ryan’s hits were home runs.

Therefore, neither player hit home runs on more than half of their hits.

Now, let’s see more concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "fbb4d977-7db5-579e-baf0-bb8e13b6c15a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14935 :tutorial/title "Comparing Decimals and Percents in Context"} :step/id #uuid "4ce04142-5c86-5b4c-a76f-55af88901484" :step/math-academy-id 632749 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148486}} {:db/id 17592186148486 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147544 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147235 :question/id #uuid "4016fd3c-d8b2-5ef2-8554-47ac5c183950" :question/math-academy-id "e-22017"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "638e604b-5416-5d3c-a61f-5be645aa255b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147801} {:db/id 17592186147802} {:db/id 17592186434388}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements in Context"} :step/id #uuid "c0e51654-69d7-5097-b27f-71f3c28bce97" :step/math-academy-id 632750 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148487}} {:db/id 17592186148487 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148671 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose Carlos and Henry have the same number of trading cards. A total of $32 \%$ of Carlos's cards are rare cards, while

$$
\dfrac{1}{4}
$$

of Henry's cards are rare cards.

Who has more rare cards?

To answer this, we need to *compare the fraction and the percentage*:

$$
\dfrac{1}{4} \qquad\text{and}\qquad 32 \%
$$

A common method is to convert the fraction to a percentage.

First, we write

$$
\dfrac{1}{4}
$$

as an equivalent fraction with $100$ as the denominator:

$$
\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1 \times 25}{4 \times 25} = \dfrac{25}{100}
$$

Now, we can write this fraction as a percentage:

$$
\dfrac{25}{100} = 25 \%
$$

Since $25 \% < 32 \%$, we can conclude that Carlos has *more* rare cards than Carlos." :tutorial/id #uuid "4be68676-8fcc-56ce-a8ef-96b2a954a03c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14937 :tutorial/title "Comparing Fractions and Percents in Context"} :step/id #uuid "99330381-c770-5a62-a3c7-a79ba13fcd0b" :step/math-academy-id 632753 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148488}} {:db/id 17592186148488 :step/content {:db/id 17592186147545 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186147247 :question/id #uuid "e6b550b1-cd66-5a70-9d11-d37733ac4c5f" :question/math-academy-id "e-2319"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9d39373d-ba41-53aa-8119-4ecf5138a50a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186147799} {:db/id 17592186147800} {:db/id 17592186424830}] :knowledge-point/title "Comparing Fractions and Percents: Word Problem"} :step/id #uuid "5102e680-a474-5349-a6c9-27bc67303b7a" :step/math-academy-id 632754}] :activity/title "Comparing Fractions, Percents, and Decimals" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186147658} {:db/id 17592186148482 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148698 :tutorial/content "When working with fractions, percents, and decimals, we often need to decide which number is greater or smaller. For example:

$$
{\color{purple}-\dfrac{1}{2}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{2}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{3}}, \quad {\color{purple}-\dfrac{2}{3}}, \quad {\color{purple}\dfrac{2}{3}}
$$

Every integer is also a rational number because every integer can be expressed as a ratio of two integers. For example,

$$
{\color{blue}2} = {\color{black}\dfrac{2}{1}}, \qquad {\color{red}-9} = {\color{black}\dfrac{(-9)}{\phantom{-}1}}
$$

Likewise, any mixed number is a rational number because it can be written as an improper fraction. For example,

$$
2 \, \dfrac{1}{3}
$$

is a rational number because

$$
2 \, \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 + 1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}
$$

We can now add the rational numbers to our inclusion diagram.

![](images/12/124ced6b317bdd2df4f967e6ea45e613b89d9fa136acb5edf8f7ed86fa8a4c06.png)

Notice that the integers (and therefore the natural numbers) are contained within the rational numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "3563ca37-8d82-5742-92b2-bb3918a71477" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9071 :tutorial/title "The Rational Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "cc715ab1-8b8b-555b-bd73-97d8d33107c0" :step/math-academy-id 172688 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153007}} {:db/id 17592186153007 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152126 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151861 :question/id #uuid "471f680f-5a51-5dac-aa3c-834610690f0e" :question/math-academy-id "e-14644"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f7063140-eebe-598c-b530-3c13509d359b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152877} {:db/id 17592186152878} {:db/id 17592186424829} {:db/id 17592186433607} {:db/id 17592186433608}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Numbers as Rational"} :step/id #uuid "ba79c281-b939-528f-8605-0a6cd2aa6abd" :step/math-academy-id 172689 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153008}} {:db/id 17592186153008 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153468 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following rational number:

$$
\dfrac13
$$

We can find the decimal representation of this rational number by dividing $1$ by $3$ using long division, as follows:

| $\,\,0 \,. 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3$$\:\ldots$$3$$\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\,. \,} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0}$$-\!\!\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$0$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$1$$\,\ldots$ |
| --- |

Note that, in this case

- the long division process never ends, and
- the digit $3$ after the decimal point repeats *forever*.

Therefore, we have that

$$
\dfrac13 = 0.333\,333\ldots
$$

This is an example of a **repeating decimal**. A repeating decimal is a decimal where the digits after the decimal point continue forever but in a repeating pattern.

It's convenient to use the following special notation to indicate decimals that repeat indefinitely.

$$
0.\overline{3} = 0.333\,333\ldots
$$

Some decimals have two or more digits that repeat indefinitely. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.78^(―) &= 0.78787878… \\
0.675^(―) &= 0.675675675…
\end{aligned}
$$

Some repeating decimals have non-repeating digits before the repeating part. For example:

$$
0.333\overline{67} = 0.333\,67\,67\,67\,67\ldots
$$

The key takeaway for this section is that every repeating decimal is rational! In other words, every repeating decimal can be expressed as a ratio of two integers.

For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.3^(―) &= \frac{1}{3} \\
0.78^(―) &= \frac{26}{33} \\
0.33367^(―) &= \frac{16517}{49500}
\end{aligned}
$$

In a future lesson, we'll learn how to express a repeating decimal as a fraction. [{:db/id 17592186172716 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173299 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we studied some rules for determining if an integer is divisible by $2,5,10,4,$ and $8.$ In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding of divisibility rules to include $3,9,6,$ and $7.$

We have the following rule for determining if a number is divisible by $3{:}$

*A number is divisible by $3$ if the sum of its digits is divisible by $3.$*

For example, let's determine if the following number is divisible by $3{:}$

$$
312\,561
$$

If we sum the digits, we get

$$
3+1+2+5+6+1 = 18.
$$

Now, since $18$ is divisible by $3,$ we conclude that $312\,561$ is divisible by $3.$

The rule for determining if a number is divisible by $9$ is similar:

*A number is divisible by $9$ if the sum of its digits is divisible by $9.$*

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "0b0f6b89-66c8-5e63-9825-60eb62f1271f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9390 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1794b655-2bac-5203-8fdb-02da477fb69d" :step/math-academy-id 172668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172717}} {:db/id 17592186172717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186171932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171756 :question/id #uuid "b926f4d4-513a-5b05-8ce2-bedc39784ada" :question/math-academy-id "e-15012"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fb8fa39c-a982-569a-b2e0-833c51259711" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048145} {:db/id 17592186048967}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172310} {:db/id 17592186172602} {:db/id 17592186432788} {:db/id 17592186432792} {:db/id 17592186432793} {:db/id 17592186432794}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining if a Number Is Divisible by 3 or 9"} :step/id #uuid "b30e2ba3-941c-5d16-b861-02db07423b35" :step/math-academy-id 172669 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172718}} {:db/id 17592186172718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173304 :tutorial/content "We have the following rule for determining if a number is divisible by $6{:}$

*A number is divisible by $6$ if it is divisible by both $2$ and $3.$*

For example, let's determine if the following number is divisible by $6{:}$

$$
353,856

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055836 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055942 :tutorial/content "The **Cartesian coordinate system** (or **Cartesian plane**) is a grid that we can use to understand where certain objects lie, similar to a map. This grid looks as follows:

![](images/fd/fd702a53ff1127a2432cbdd9a3c7057a08c73ac7a086454c066fa2c96bea7974.png)

It consists of a horizontal number line called the **$x$-axis** and a vertical number line called the **$y$-axis**.

The **origin** is the location where the $x$ and $y$ axes meet and is given the symbol $O.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dacc8373-6186-517b-bba8-ec1729732e4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1431 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5cca38c5-c625-5a28-92d3-ccdcc09f108d" :step/math-academy-id 607419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055837}} {:db/id 17592186055837 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055943 :tutorial/content "Every location on the Cartesian plane is called a **point**. Every point is identified using an $x$**-coordinate** and a $y$**-coordinate**. Together, points are expressed using an **ordered pair** of **coordinates** $(x,y).$

For example, we can mark (or **plot**) the point $A$ with coordinates $({\color{red}{3}},{\color{blue}{2}})$ by starting from $O$ and then traveling $\color{red}3$ units towards the right, followed $\color{blue}2$ units up.

![](images/c1/c1ef61dedbbcc6eedcd125c2c62cdfbaa4d9b9a12f10181714b51c060a059fd3.png)

We say that

- the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $3$,

- the $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $2$,

- the $xy$-coordinates (or just "the coordinates") of $A$ are $(3,2).$

The letter $A$ is just a label for our point. It's usually a good idea to label points!" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e7847c5-757a-5cb8-b947-9c7d806b5dc5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1432 :tutorial/title "Coordinates and Ordered Pairs"} :step/id #uuid "b81ec1ae-2147-51bf-abd0-42837ec9335a" :step/math-academy-id 607420 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055838}} {:db/id 17592186055838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055957 :tutorial/content "Remember that a coordinate plane is made by two number lines that meet at $0.$ Since these are number lines, we can extend both to include negative numbers.

![](images/f1/f1eeb7f3bc0ab8b39e9dc7127d76a32f1dd130d380748fedc6e11b967f3878ed.png)

We plot an ordered pair $({\color{red}x},{\color{blue}y})$ similar to before, but if the number is negative, we reverse the direction. So, starting at the origin:

- if the first number is positive, move that number of places *right* along the $\color{red}x$-axis. If its negative, move *left*.

- if the second number is positive, move that number of places *up* along the $\color{blue}y$-axis. If its negative, move *down*.

To demonstrate, let's find the coordinates of the point $Q$ above.

To find the coordinates of $Q,$ we start at the origin, move $\color{red}3$ units *left*, and then $\color{blue}2$ units *down*. 

![](images/b4/b4f58f0c1ad6dc2936ed1b24c844fa82c1b1d5ec10c80e14c6a43f6f4eaf5544.png)

Since we move left, the $\color{red}x$-coordinate is negative, and since we move down, the $\color{blue}y$-coordinate is negative.

Therefore, the coordinates of $Q$ are $({\color{red}{-3}},{\color{blue}{-2}}).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7383452c-9470-5f05-b206-dffbb84808dd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2092 :tutorial/title "Extending the - the top-right quadrant the first quadrant (I),

- the top-left is the second quadrant (II),

- the bottom-left is the third quadrant (III),

- and and bottom-right is the fourth quadrant (IV).

![](images/c1/c1ef61dedbbcc6eedcd125c2c62cdfbaa4d9b9a12f10181714b51c060a059fd3.png)

We say that

- the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $3$,

- the $y$-coordinate of $A$ is $2$,

- the $xy$-coordinates (or just "the coordinates") of $A$ are $(3,2).$

The letter $A$ is just a label for our point. It's usually a good idea to label points!" :tutorial/id #uuid "9e7847c5-757a-5cb8-b947-9c7d806b5dc5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1432 :tutorial/title "Coordinates and Ordered Pairs"} {:db/id 17592186055838 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055957 :tutorial/content "Remember that a coordinate plane is made by two number lines that meet at $0.$ Since these are number lines, we can extend both to include negative numbers.

We plot an ordered pair $({\color{red}x},{\color{blue}y})$ similar to before, but if the number is negative, we reverse the direction. So, starting at the origin:

- if the first number is positive, move that number of places *right* along the $\color{red}x$-axis. If its negative, move *left*.

- if the second number is positive, move that number of places *up* along the $\color{blue}y$-axis. If its negative, move *down*.

To demonstrate, let's find the coordinates of the point $Q$ above.

To find the coordinates of $Q,$ we start at the origin, move $\color{red}3$ units *left*, and then $\color{blue}2$ units *down*.

For example, the letters

$$
x, \quad y, \quad z, \quad a, \quad b, \quad c, \quad k, \quad m,\quad n,\quad p, \quad q,\quad r, \quad \ldots
$$

are commonly used as variables. But in general, we can use any letter we like.

An **algebraic expression** is a combination of variables with mathematical operations, like addition $(+)$, subtraction $(-)$, multiplication $(\times)$, and division $(\div).$ So 

$$
x+2,\qquad 6-y,\qquad 2\times p + 1,\qquad q\div r,
$$

are all examples of algebraic expressions." :tutorial/id #uuid "232cd5fe-049f-512d-8d7c-ad600a7e6a81" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8165 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid We know that the derivative of the hyperbolic sine is the hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sinh{x}) = \cosh{x}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we have

$$
\int \cosh{x}\,\textrm d x = \sinh{x} + C.
$$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\cosh x) = \sinh{x} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \int \sinh x\  \textrm{d}x = \cosh x + C.

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 5+4t , 3-2t, -4-3t \rangle.

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-7,5,1⟩ & =-65 \\ ⟨5+4t,3-2t,-4-3t⟩\cdot ⟨-7,5,1⟩ & =-65 \\ -7(5+4t)+5(3-2t)+(-4-3t) & =-65 \\ -35-28t+15-10t-4-3t & =-65 \\ -41t & =-41 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the position vector $\mathbf{p}$ of the intersection point is obtained by substituting $t=1$ into the equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨5+4(1),3-2(1),-4-3(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨9,1,-7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨5,3,-4⟩+t⟨-5,2,7⟩,\,Π:r\cdot ⟨2,3,1⟩=30.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's write the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨5-5t,3+2t,-4+7t⟩.
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨5-5t,3+2t,-4+7t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨2,3,1⟩ & =30 \\ ⟨5-5t,3+2t,-4+7t⟩\cdot ⟨2,3,1⟩ & =30 \\ 2(5-5t)+3(3+2t)-4+7t & =30 \\ 10-10t+9+6t-4+7t & =30 \\ 3t & =15 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$ is obtained by substituting $t=5$ into the equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨5-5(5),3+2(5),-4+7(5)⟩ \\  & =⟨-20,13,31⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(-20,13,31).$"} {:db/id 17592186342124 :question/id #uuid "b7b7455d-19c2-5862-8ffa-6bf81d08e53f" :question/math-academy-id "q-73985" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119836 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abef3da6-252e-51e4-b816-9ef7233b9a5d" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Intersection Point of a Line in Vector Form and a Plane in Dot Product Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2280cb71-d56d-5c11-9ffc-9e7ac8621681" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-17,-10,13)" :db/id 17592186339424} {:answer/id #uuid "51d70f39-09be-5fe0-b06a-f48d5b7f85d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186339879} {:answer/id #uuid "7923bb17-a47c-5f0f-aa70-02c9163dfd5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-13,-10,17)" :db/id 17592186340209} {:answer/id #uuid "a3365d47-2432-5573-a0bc-2a03360f17ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-3,0,1)" :db/id 17592186340608} {:answer/id #uuid "ed6d6aad-b4fa-596f-8dd5-f5bc35997084" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-10,-13,7)" :db/id 17592186341222}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "7923bb17-a47c-5f0f-aa70-02c9163dfd5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-13,-10,17)" :db/id 17592186340209} :answer-field/id #uuid "0ab4e761-07dd-58e8-b46a-0567acd50ed3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186341400}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$

$$

Finally, position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$ is obtained by substituting $t=-5$ into the equation of the line, as follows:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Finally, position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$ is obtained by substituting $t=-2$ into the equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨1+5(-2),1+2(-2),1-4(-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨-9,-3,9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-2,1,4⟩ & =11 \\ ⟨2-t,3+2t,-1+3t⟩\cdot ⟨-2,1,4⟩ & =11 \\ -2(2-t)+1(3+2t)+4(-1+3t) & =11 \\ -4+2t+3+2t-4+12t & =11 \\ 16t & =16 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$ is obtained by substituting $t=1$ into the equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2-1,3+2(1),-1+3(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,5,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(1,5,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186399615 :question/id #uuid "8e5fe668-3628-59a7-b261-da619f1e8497" :question/math-academy-id "q-108310"} {:db/id 17592186403738 $$
l: \mathbf{r} = \langle 1,3,1 \rangle + t \langle 2,1,0 \rangle, \qquad  \Pi:4x-3y+2z-7 = 0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle 1+2t , 3+t, 1 \rangle .
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-3y+2z-7 & =0 \\ 4x-3y+2z & =7 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,2⟩ & =7 \\ r\cdot ⟨4,-3,2⟩ & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $\mathbf{r} = \langle 1+2t , 3+t, 1 \rangle$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨4,-3,2⟩ & =7 \\ ⟨1+2t,3+t,1⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,2⟩ & =7 \\ 4(1+2t)-3(3+t)+2\cdot 1 & =7 \\ 4+8t-9-3t+2 & =7 \\ 5t & =10 \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $\mathbf{p}$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨1+2(2),3+(2),1⟩ \\  & =⟨5,5,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(5 , 5, 1).$"} {:db/id 17592186048729} {:db/id 17592186120229 :question/id #uuid "a9c8b702-f6a3-5488-9345-1b22f3aeec01" :question/math-academy-id "q-33081"} 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨2,1,0⟩+t⟨1,3,2⟩,\,Π:3x-2y+4z+6=0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨2+t,1+3t,2t⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2y+4z+6 & =0 \\ 3x-2y+4z & =-6 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨3,-2,4⟩ & =-6 \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-2,4⟩ & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨2+t,1+3t,2t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,-2,4⟩ & =-6 \\ ⟨2+t,1+3t,2t⟩\cdot ⟨3,-2,4⟩ & =-6 \\ 3(2+t)-2(1+3t)+4(2t) & =-6 \\ 6+3t-2-6t+8t & =-6 \\ 5t & =-10 \\ t & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-2$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2+(-2),1+3(-2),2(-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(0,-5,-4).$"} {:db/id 17592186304967 :question/id #uuid "00b27684-fae1-56d0-a859-d1fc21cc59df" :question/math-academy-id "q-33197"} {:db/id 17592186304971 :question/id #uuid "c249fd8c-dcff-5201-89e1-bb6d2a206072" :question/math-academy-id "q-33201"} {:db/id 17592186314820 :question/id #uuid "5873c215-84fe-562e-9b4f-b99d76cb6e63" :question/math-academy-id "q-33968"} {:db/id 17592186342129 :question/id #uuid "156769fc-4325-56fe-a6f3-a488d1baa118" :question/math-academy-id "q-74004" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8e017315-e476-5fa0-8361-dc00652a6489" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,0,1)" :db/id 17592186340405} {:answer/id #uuid "ad64653c-387b-56c4-988a-77711f82ccae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186340706} {:answer/id #uuid "af463bcf-e431-5d1e-a420-7660e1b98031" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2,-5,4)" :db/id 17592186340726} {:answer/id #uuid "d8153fa3-e604-533d-b56e-b26114f3d4d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3,1,5)" :db/id 17592186341045} {:answer/id #uuid "f86bd550-c5e7-5c4a-ad94-8436818324a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-5,4,2)" :db/id 17592186341326}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341045} :answer-field/id #uuid "9343b686-98f1-53b8-a0c6-e7d798a3b52a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341638}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩,\,Π:r=⟨-5,4,2⟩+s⟨0,3,1⟩+t⟨2,0,1⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨0,3,1⟩\times ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =3i+2j-6k \\  & =⟨3,2,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =⟨-5,4,2⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ ⟨3-2w,1-5w,5+4w⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ 3(3-2w)+2(1-5w)-6(5+4w) & =-19 \\ 9-6w+2-10w-30-24w & =-19 \\ -40w & =0 \\ w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=0$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨3-2(0),1-5(0),5+4(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(3,1,5).$"} {:db/id 17592186399636 :question/id #uuid "0da8771f-0983-5e77-be97-afe167de38df" :question/math-academy-id "q-108371"} {:db/id 17592186399650 :question/id #uuid "2d225520-d7e9-5a28-afbf-6e16563a3611" :question/math-academy-id "q-108889" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119837 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "caf29808-4551-56a0-ac86-a4587a06fc0f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Intersection Point of a Line and a Plane Given in Other Forms"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c181d54f-7b5e-5e40-b660-5db606239a3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(13,7,2)" :db/id 17592186399652} {:answer/id #uuid "7c2c2f01-60e6-5197-ae47-76dd272575a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(8,3,-1)" :db/id 17592186399653} {:answer/id #uuid "100fc206-faa0-5c9a-8c1d-f828c27459ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-12,-5,-13)" :db/id 17592186399654} {:answer/id #uuid "a03ac96b-8e87-5579-959e-6059ecf3486c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-7,-3,-10)" :db/id 17592186399655} {:answer/id #uuid "d6d8eeca-91ef-5d44-a9a1-da7d1707ffce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186399656}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "100fc206-faa0-5c9a-8c1d-f828c27459ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(-12,-5,-13)" :db/id 17592186399654} :answer-field/id #uuid "3cd4a0b3-55ce-54d3-98c8-8b7021d46e30" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186399651}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:\frac{x-3}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+4}{3},\,Π:r\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩=39.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of the line $l$, we know that it passes through the point $A(3,1,-4)$ and it is parallel to the vector $v=⟨5,2,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨3,1,-4⟩+t⟨5,2,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Now, substituting $r=⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩ & =39 \\ ⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩ & =39 \\ (-3)(3+5t)+2(1+2t)-(-4+3t) & =39 \\ -9-15t+2+4t+4-3t & =39 \\ -14t & =42 \\ t & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-3$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨3+5(-3),1+2(-3),-4+3(-3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-12,-5,-13⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $P(-12,-5,-13).$"} {:db/id 17592186402093 :question/id #uuid "eaab1f60-24fb-5572-8cfb-474f418bf09f" :question/math-academy-id "q-33205"} {:db/id 17592186402256 :question/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨1,-1,2⟩+w⟨3,4,-1⟩,\,Π:r=⟨5,3,-4⟩+s⟨1,0,2⟩+t⟨0,-2,3⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨1,0,2⟩\times ⟨0,-2,3⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =4i-3j-2k \\  & =⟨4,-3,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =⟨5,3,-4⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨1,-1,2⟩+w⟨3,4,-1⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19 \\ ⟨1+3w,-1+4w,2-w⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19 \\ 4(1+3w)-3(-1+4w)-2(2-w) & =19 \\ 4+12w+3-12w-4+2w & =19 \\ 2w & =16 \\ w & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=8$ into the equation of the line:

$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨2,0,2⟩\times ⟨1,4,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-8i+2j+8k \\  & =⟨-8,2,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =⟨-15,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨2,3,1⟩+w⟨-3,-2,3⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130 \\ ⟨2-3w,3-2w,1+3w⟩\cdot ⟨-8,2,8⟩ & =130 \\ -8(2-3w)+2(3-2w)+8(1+3w) & =130 \\ -16+24w+6-4w+8+24w & =130 \\ 44w & =132 \\ w & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=3$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨2-3(3),3-2(3),1+3(3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-7,-3,10⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(-7,-3,10).$"} {:db/id 17592186119838 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119652 :question/id #uuid "f952e670-a673-5c15-913b-c396e8885142" $$

To get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$, we substitute $t=6$ into the parametric equations of the line:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2-2(7)=-16 \\ y=5-3(7)=-16 \\ z=-1+2(7)=13\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/math-academy-id 1808} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120720 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121053 :tutorial/content "Consider the following equations of a line $l$ and a plane $\Pi\mathbin{:}$

$$
l: \mathbf{r} = \langle 2,2,1 \rangle + t \langle 3,0,1 \rangle, \qquad \Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 3,-5,1 \rangle = 7.
$$

How can we find the intersection point $P$ of $l$ and $\Pi?$

We start by writing the equation of the line in the form $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle.$ Now, since $P$ must lie on the line $l,$ we can write its coordinates as $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ for some particular value of $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

![](images/d3/d3ba164eb98a53c463744e11d6593177ddde2a0a309f752e5d86b30db0d79925.png)

On the other hand, $P$ also lies on the plane $\Pi.$ So, the coordinates $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ must satisfy the equation of the plane as well. Substituting the position vector $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle$ into the equation of the plane and solving for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ ⟨2+3t,2,1+t⟩\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ 3(2+3t)-5\cdot 2+(1+t) & =7 \\ 6+9t-10+1+t & =7 \\ 10t & =10 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $\mathbf{p}$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2+3(1),2,1+(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨5,2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(5, 2, 2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b2ca8cb0-0b92-5b99-ac8b-edd2f2a6dbb1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3259 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Consider the following equations of a line $l$ and a plane $\Pi\mathbin{:}$

$$
l: \mathbf{r} = \langle 2,2,1 \rangle + t \langle 3,0,1 \rangle, \qquad \Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 3,-5,1 \rangle = 7.
$$

How can we find the intersection point $P$ of $l$ and $\Pi?$

We start by writing the equation of the line in the form $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle.$ Now, since $P$ must lie on the line $l,$ we can write its coordinates as $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ for some particular value of $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

![](images/d3/d3ba164eb98a53c463744e11d6593177ddde2a0a309f752e5d86b30db0d79925.png)

On the other hand, $P$ also lies on the plane $\Pi.$ So, the coordinates $P(2+3t , 2, 1+t)$ must satisfy the equation of the plane as well. Substituting the position vector $\mathbf{r} = \langle 2+3t , 2, 1+t \rangle$ into the equation of the plane and solving for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ ⟨2+3t,2,1+t⟩\cdot ⟨3,-5,1⟩ & =7 \\ 3(2+3t)-5\cdot 2+(1+t) & =7 \\ 6+9t-10+1+t & =7 \\ 10t & =10 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $\mathbf{p}$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=1$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨2+3(1),2,1+(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨5,2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(5, 2, 2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b2ca8cb0-0b92-5b99-ac8b-edd2f2a6dbb1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3259 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a814365d-ddd3-5356-ac6d-30d046db60e2" :step/math-academy-id 17931 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120721}} {:db/id 17592186121053 :tutorial/content "Consider the following equations of a line $l$ and a plane $\Pi\mathbin{:}$

"Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩,\,Π:r=⟨-5,4,2⟩+s⟨0,3,1⟩+t⟨2,0,1⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨0,3,1⟩\times ⟨2,0,1⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =3i+2j-6k \\  & =⟨3,2,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =⟨-5,4,2⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨3,1,5⟩+w⟨-2,-5,4⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ ⟨3-2w,1-5w,5+4w⟩\cdot ⟨3,2,-6⟩ & =-19 \\ 3(3-2w)+2(1-5w)-6(5+4w) & =-19 \\ 9-6w+2-10w-30-24w & =-19 \\ -40w & =0 \\ w & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=0$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨3-2(0),1-5(0),5+4(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,1,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(3,1,5).$"} :step/id #uuid "0227058d-e862-5e31-b5c8-bea4849a37b5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484327}} {:db/id 17592186484313 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342127 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b2ccf68-fbc4-58ea-80f0-c47a1f4e61c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186339365} {:answer/id #uuid "1d364631-26c0-59a4-93c9-0842ba8027a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(19,10,16)" :db/id 17592186339381} {:answer/id #uuid "2bfe2f6a-4b05-5041-9be9-ec95d41ced84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(18,8,12)" :db/id 17592186339510} {:answer/id #uuid "90fc5ea2-94e0-5824-91af-e274368bde07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(18,11,16)" :db/id 17592186340429} {:answer/id #uuid "a5f82de1-4dec-5d15-9285-344580d1aa1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(8,-1,6)" :db/id 17592186340633}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340429} :answer-field/id #uuid "3769c405-5ffb-59ea-8180-d6fbf6837b56" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341479}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8a17e320-306c-50fa-b84b-f8cbe958e629" :question/math-academy-id "q-73993" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$" :question/worked-solution "We can substitute the parametric expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ of the line into the equation of the plane immediately:

$$

To get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$, we substitute $t=-3$ into the parametric equations of the line:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=3-5(-3)=18 \\ y=2-3(-3)=11 \\ z=-2-6(-3)=16\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is  $P(18,11,16).$"} :step/id #uuid "3315e388-6b5a-5594-b5f3-c37c6118ed26" :step/next {:db/id 17592186484300}} {:db/id 17592186484327 :step/content {:db/id 17592186475912 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "007d69dc-a2ca-580f-b0f7-74cbcfa1ebdd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186475444} {:answer/id #uuid "3a25e529-3954-5987-92eb-d533381cc44b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(25,31,-6)" :db/id 17592186475523} {:answer/id #uuid "52af092c-e727-5f18-8ff7-345347fe6d51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-8,-13,5)" :db/id 17592186475562} {:answer/id #uuid "572842f6-cb5d-5a22-b2c9-50266f22eb6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(13,15,-2)" :db/id 17592186475570} {:answer/id #uuid "fca47535-789f-5b0b-98b2-271a04ca1b25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-14,-21,7)" :db/id 17592186475823}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186475523} :answer-field/id #uuid "d8937436-576e-5320-a137-6b981c96167e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186475895}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "07e33caa-9650-5834-8d9a-46cc82f723d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-108434" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨1,-1,2⟩+w⟨3,4,-1⟩,\,Π:r=⟨5,3,-4⟩+s⟨1,0,2⟩+t⟨0,-2,3⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vectors to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨1,0,2⟩\times ⟨0,-2,3⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =4i-3j-2k \\  & =⟨4,-3,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =⟨5,3,-4⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨1,-1,2⟩+w⟨3,4,-1⟩$ into the equation of the plane in dot product form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19 \\ ⟨1+3w,-1+4w,2-w⟩\cdot ⟨4,-3,-2⟩ & =19 \\ 4(1+3w)-3(-1+4w)-2(2-w) & =19 \\ 4+12w+3-12w-4+2w & =19 \\ 2w & =16 \\ w & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $q$ of the intersection point $Q,$ we substitute $w=8$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}q & =⟨1+3(8),-1+4(8),2-8⟩ \\  & =⟨25,31,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $Q(25,31,-6).$"} :step/id #uuid "6a1f4ccb-dfb0-5de6-aea8-7109eb01b3fc"} {:db/id 17592186484330 :step/content {:db/id 17592186484201 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20fc86f8-0368-54eb-a3e0-3cf6b0379332" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-16,-16,13)" :db/id 17592186483621} {:answer/id #uuid "2143e54b-67d5-5002-957a-3bf88c230ca4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(24,-11,11)" :db/id 17592186483624} {:answer/id #uuid "257b548a-b52d-5b2d-8a2f-57d74b50d39c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No intersection" :db/id 17592186483630} {:answer/id #uuid "7944f3e7-3b31-5e5a-b5cb-a1562208eb42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(11,-13,11)" :db/id 17592186483813} {:answer/id #uuid "a0a4f2b9-c6e0-5e67-8ab6-66d592472d45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(26,12,12)" :db/id 17592186483899}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186483621} :answer-field/id #uuid "15f90597-4c03-5ae4-b2c2-f42eae091087" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186484091}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "12b4f5c6-720f-5c2c-b1e8-295eb7dcb29c" :question/math-academy-id "q-73991" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.

- let $A$ be the event that the selected worker works department $A,$

- let $B$ be the event that the selected worker works department $B,$

- let $C$ be the event that the selected worker works department $C.$

Then the disjoint union $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ covers the entire sample space.

Recall that the law of total probability states that

$$
P(F) = P(F \cap A) + P(F \cap B) + P(F \cap C).
$$

We wish to find $P(F \cap B)\mathbin{:}$

- To calculate $P(F \cap A),$ we take the number of females who work in department $A$ $(7)$ and divide by the total number of workers $(40).$ So, we have 

$$
P(F \cap A) = \dfrac{7}{40}.
$$

- To calculate $P(F \cap C),$ we take the number of females who work in department $C$ $(8)$ and divide by the total number of workers $(40).$ So, we have

$$
P(F \cap C) = \dfrac{8}{40}.
$$

- Also, we're given that

$$
P(F) = \dfrac{21}{40}.
$$

Finally, substituting the above information into the law of total probability and solving for $P(F \cap B),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(F) & =P(F\cap A)+P(F\cap B)+P(F\cap C) \\ \frac{21}{40} & =\frac{7}{40}+P(F\cap B)+\frac{8}{40} \\ P(F\cap B) & =\frac{21}{40}-\frac{7}{40}-\frac{8}{40}. \\ P(F\cap B) & =\frac{6}{40} \\ P(F\cap B) & =\frac{3}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186091926 1069 "e-10110" 17592186045417] [17592186091926 1071 "Three factories produce the same spare part for a particular car model. To calculate the probability that a randomly selected part is defective, we can use the law of total probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D\cap A)+P(D\cap B)+P(D\cap C) \\  & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation.

- Since Factory ${A}$ produces $32\%$ of the parts, Factory ${B}$ produces $33 \%$ of the parts, and Factory ${C}$ produces $35 \%$ of the parts, we have

$$
P(A) = 0.32, \qquad P(B) = 0.33, \qquad P(C)=0.35.
$$

- Since $1.5\%$ of the parts produced by Factory ${A},$ $2\%$ of the parts produced by Factory ${B},$ and $1.4\%$ of the parts produced by Factory ${C}$ are defective, we have 

$$
P(D | A) = 0.015, \qquad P(D | B) = 0.02, \qquad P(D | C) = 0.014.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability, the probability that a randomly selected part is defective is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(D) & =P(D|A)P(A)+P(D|B)P(B)+P(D|C)P(C) \\  & =(0.015)(0.32)+(0.02)(0.33)+(0.014)(0.35) \\  & =0.004\,8+0.006\,6+0.004\,9 \\  & =0.016\,3.\end{aligned}

Then the disjoint union $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ covers the entire sample space. 

To calculate the probability of selecting a red apple, we can use the law of total probability: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =P(R\cap A)+P(R\cap B)+P(R\cap C) \\  & =P(R|A)P(A)+P(R|B)P(B)+P(R|C)P(C)\end{aligned}
$$

Let's go through the problem statement and translate each piece of information into mathematical notation.

- Since a basket is randomly selected and there are $3$ baskets, we have

$$
P(A) = P(B) = P(C) = \dfrac{1}{3}.
$$

- Since $\dfrac25$ of the apples in basket $A$ and $\dfrac14$ of the apples in basket $B$ are red, we have

$$
P(R | A)= \dfrac25, \qquad P(R | B) = \dfrac14.
$$

- Since the probability of picking a red apple from any of the three baskets is $\dfrac13,$ we have

$$
P(R) = \dfrac13.
$$

Substituting the above information into the law of total probability and solving for $P(R|C),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R) & =P(R|A)P(A)+P(R|B)P(B)+P(R|C)P(C) \\ \frac{1}{3} & =(\frac{2}{5})(\frac{1}{3})+(\frac{1}{4})(\frac{1}{3})+P(R|C)(\frac{1}{3}) \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{2}{15}+\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{15}-\frac{1}{12} \\ \frac{1}{3}\cdot P(R|C) & =\frac{7}{60} \\ P(R|C) & =\frac{7}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

When these two conditions are satisfied, we say that $\mathcal S$ is the **disjoint union** of  $B_1, B_2,$ and $B_3,$ and we write 
 

$$

$$

Now suppose that we wish to compute the probability of an event $A$ that lies within $\mathcal S.$ Let's draw this event on our diagram and label its intersections with $B_1, B_2, B_3\mathbin{:}$

The **law of total probability** can be deduced from this diagram. It states that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A\cap {B}_{1})+P(A\cap {B}_{2})+P(A\cap {B}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

In this lesson, we will only consider a disjoint union of $\mathcal S$ consisting of three events. However, it should be noted that the law of total probability can be extended to an arbitrary number of events, that is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A\cap {B}_{1})+P(A\cap {B}_{2})+⋯ \\  & ={\sum }_{i}P(A\cap {B}_{i})\end{aligned}
$$

Often, it's more helpful to express this law using conditional probabilities. 

From the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cap {B}_{1}) & =P(A|{B}_{1})P({B}_{1}) \\ P(A\cap {B}_{2}) & =P(A|{B}_{2})P({B}_{2}) \\ P(A\cap {B}_{3}) & =P(A|{B}_{3})P({B}_{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above form into the law of total probability, we get

$$
P(A) = P(A|B_1)P(B_1)+  P(A|B_2)P(B_2) +  P(A|B_3)P(B_3).
$$

What is the probability that a randomly selected rose from the garden is red?

Let $A$ be the event that a chosen rose is red, and 

- let $B_1$ be the event that the selected rose comes from the first plot,

- let $B_2$ be the event that the selected rose comes from the second plot,

- let $B_3$ be the event that the selected rose comes from the third plot.

Notice that the disjoint union

$$
B_1\sqcup B_2\sqcup B_3
$$

covers the entire sample space, and that there are a total of 

$$
10+12+14=36
$$

roses in the garden. 

- To calculate $P(A \cap B_1),$ we take the number of red roses in the first plot $(5)$ and divide by the total number of roses $(36).$ So, we have 

$$
P(A \cap B_1) = \dfrac{5}{36}.
$$

- To calculate $P(A \cap B_2),$ we take the number of red roses in the second plot $(6)$ and divide by the total number of roses $(36).$ So, we have 

$$
P(A \cap B_2) = \dfrac{6}{36}.
$$

- To calculate $P(A \cap B_3),$ we take the number of red roses in the third plot $(4)$ and divide by the total number of roses $(36).$ So, we have 

$$
P(A \cap B_3) = \dfrac{4}{36}.
$$

So, to calculate the probability that a randomly chosen rose is red, we use the law of total probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =P(A\cap {B}_{1})+P(A\cap {B}_{2})+P(A\cap {B}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{36}+\frac{6}{36}+\frac{4}{36} \\  & =\frac{15}{36} \\  & =\frac{5}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

"Consider the recursive sequence given by the formula

$$
a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n, \quad a_1 = {\color{blue}{1}}, \quad a_2 = {\color{red}{3}},\quad n \geq 1
$$

As we know, to calculate the next term in a recursive sequence, we need to use the previous terms. However, unlike what we've seen before, this time, we need to use *two* previous terms to calculate the next term.

We already know $a_1$ and $a_2$, so let's calculate $a_3$. We do this by substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1 + 2} &= a_{1 + 1} + a_{1} \\
a_{3} &= a_{2} + a_{1} \\
a_{3} &= 3 + 1 \\
a_{3} &= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know $a_3$, we can calculate $a_4$ in the same way, by substituting $n=2$ into the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{2 + 2} &= a_{2 + 1} + a_{2} \\
a_{4} &= a_{3} + a_{2} \\
a_{4} &= 4 + 3 \\
a_{4} &= 7
\end{aligned}
$$

We can keep going by substituting $n=3, 4, 5$, and so on. The resulting terms of the sequence are as follows:

$$
1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, 29, \ldots
$$

**Note:** The recursive rule

$$
a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n
$$

gives us the **Fibonacci sequence** if we take $a_1=a_2=1$.

Recursive sequences that follow the rule

$$
a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n
$$

but have different values for $a_1$ and $a_2$ are called *variants* of the Fibonacci sequence. So the sequence that we computed above is a variant of the Fibonacci sequence with $a_1=1$ and $a_2=3$." 17592186045417] [17592186056071 1065 8905 17592186045417] [17592186056071 1066 #uuid "Consider the system of ordinary differential equations

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.

In this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.

Recall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.

As usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.

Differentiating $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φ\,u(t))^{′} \\  & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t) & =f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\Phi^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \displaystyle\int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.

"When simplifying numerical expressions, it is generally preferable to avoid having radicals in the denominator. In cases where we wish to remove a radical from a denominator, we must **rationalize the denominator**.

If the denominator of an expression consists of two terms and includes one or more radicals, we rationalize it by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the **conjugate** of the denominator.

To illustrate, consider the following expression:

$$
\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}}
$$

To find the conjugate of the denominator $1+\sqrt{2}$, we *flip the sign* between the two terms. So, the conjugate of the denominator is

$$
1\,{\color{blue}{-}}\,\sqrt{2}
$$

Now, to rationalize the denominator, we start by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate $1-\sqrt{2}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{2}} &=  \\
\frac{1}{1 + \sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{1 - \sqrt{2}}{1 - \sqrt{2}} &=  \\
(1 \cdot (1 - \sqrt{2}))/((1 + \sqrt{2})(1 - \sqrt{2})) &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{2})/((1 + \sqrt{2})(1 - \sqrt{2})) &= 
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the difference of squares formula:

$$
(a+b)(a-b) = a^2 - b^2
$$

Applying the difference of squares formula with

$$
a=1, b=\sqrt 2
$$

to simplify the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1 - \sqrt{2})/((1 + \sqrt{2})(1 - \sqrt{2})) &=  \\
(1 - \sqrt{2})/(1^{2} - (\sqrt{2})^{2}) &=  \\
\frac{1 - \sqrt{2}}{1 - 2} &=  \\
\frac{1 - \sqrt{2}}{-1} &=  \\
&= \sqrt{2} - 1
\end{aligned}

After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

- $\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean

- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score

$$

$$
\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.025.

Notice that $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ is precisely the area bounded by each "tail" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\pm z_{\alpha/2}\mathbin{:}$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.96<Z<1.96)=0.95.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\left(\overline{x} - 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\: \overline{x} + 1.96\cdot\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)

\sigma=3,
$$

we obtain that our $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is 

$$
\big( 12- 1.859, \: 12 + 1.859 \big).
$$

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?" 17592186045417] [17592186342005 1072 #uuid "80f56e91-1777-5d7a-b918-7d315f6b332a" 17592186045417] [17592186342005 1074 "A type II region can be written as

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $y:$

$$
y=-2(x-3)\,⟹\,x=-\frac{y}{2}+3
$$

The function $x=-\sqrt{y}+2$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=1$ and $y=3.$ So, we have $1\le y\le 3.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](images/fb/fb05eec73599c1beb8dd588c478208315f6edaf10af999115eb29fa10d5601e9.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=-\sqrt{y}+2$ and leaves through the upper function $x=-\frac{y}{2}+3.$ So, we have $-\sqrt{y}+2\le x\le -\frac{y}{2}+3.$

D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,-\sqrt{y}+2\le x\le -\frac{y}{2}+3}.

First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\sech x)' = -\sech x\tanh x, \quad (\csch x)' = -\csch x \coth x, \quad (\coth x)' = -\csch^2 x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results and the rules of differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(3sech x + \coth x) \\
&= 3\frac{d}{dx}(sech x) + \frac{d}{dx}(\coth x) \\
&= 3(-sech x\tanh x) + (-csch^{2} x) \\
&=-3sech x\tanh x - csch^{2} x
\end{aligned}
